Title: Navigate Setup and Review Company Information
Summary: Find administration settings and review company defaults before configuring Salesforce.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Find administration settings and review company defaults before configuring Salesforce.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience with an administrator or delegated administrator who has permission to manage these settings. Test configuration changes in a development or test org first. Available options depend on edition, licenses, and enabled features.

Steps

  1. Open the gear menu in Lightning Experience and select Setup. Use Quick Find to locate settings; use Object Manager for object-specific configuration.
  2. Search for Company Information. Review the organization name, default locale, default language, default time zone, and available user licenses. Record the organization ID when identifying this environment to your administrator.
  3. Change company defaults only after checking their effect on users. Individual users can have their own language, locale, and time-zone settings. These settings affect how dates, numbers, and times appear.
  4. Check Business Hours separately if your team uses support schedules. Company time-zone settings do not replace a configured business-hours schedule.

Verify and troubleshoot

If a Setup option is missing, check the user permissions and feature availability. Validate changes with a representative user rather than relying only on an administrator account.

Title: Create and Manage Salesforce Users
Summary: Create a user with the right license, profile, locale, and access.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Create a user with the right license, profile, locale, and access.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience with an administrator or delegated administrator who has permission to manage these settings. Test configuration changes in a development or test org first. Available options depend on edition, licenses, and enabled features.

Steps

  1. In Setup, search for Users, open Users, and select New User. Enter the required identity details and a valid email address. The username must be globally unique and use an email-style format; it does not have to match the email address.
  2. Choose a user license and a compatible profile. The license determines which capabilities can be granted. Use a minimal appropriate profile and add task-specific permissions with permission sets.
  3. Set the user time zone, locale, language, and role when required. A role supports record visibility through the role hierarchy; it is different from a profile.
  4. Save the user and assign the required permission sets. If a welcome email is needed, use the available password-generation and notification option. Complete the organization's authentication and MFA onboarding process.

Verify and troubleshoot

If creation fails, check available licenses, required fields, and duplicate usernames. Deactivate departing users rather than trying to delete them; review record ownership and automation dependencies first.

Title: Grant Access with Permission Sets
Summary: Use permission sets to grant job-specific object, field, and system permissions.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Use permission sets to grant job-specific object, field, and system permissions.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience with an administrator or delegated administrator who has permission to manage these settings. Test configuration changes in a development or test org first. Available options depend on edition, licenses, and enabled features.

Steps

  1. In Setup, search for Permission Sets and select New. Enter a descriptive label and description. Choose a license restriction only when the permission set is intended for that license; otherwise select the available unrestricted option.
  2. Open Object Settings and select an object. Enable only the object permissions required for the task, such as Read or Edit, and grant the necessary field-level access.
  3. Review any required system permissions. Save the permission set, open Manage Assignments, and assign it to the intended users. Their licenses must support the permissions.
  4. Test the task as a representative user. A permission set adds access; it does not remove permissions already granted by the profile or other permission sets. Use permission set groups when several permission sets belong to the same job function.

Verify and troubleshoot

If a record remains inaccessible, check record sharing separately. Object access, field access, and record access are distinct layers; granting one does not automatically grant all three.

Title: Create Custom Fields in Object Manager
Summary: Add a custom field with an appropriate data type, visibility, and layout placement.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Add a custom field with an appropriate data type, visibility, and layout placement.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience with an administrator or delegated administrator who has permission to manage these settings. Test configuration changes in a development or test org first. Available options depend on edition, licenses, and enabled features.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager and choose the object. Open Fields & Relationships and select New. Confirm that an existing field cannot meet the requirement before creating another one.
  2. Choose the data type based on the values to store: for example, Text, Number, Date, Checkbox, Picklist, or Lookup Relationship. Enter a clear label, length or precision where applicable, description, and help text.
  3. Set field-level security for the intended users and choose the appropriate page layouts. Save the field. If the record page uses Dynamic Forms, review the field placement and visibility in Lightning App Builder as well.
  4. Create and edit a test record as a target user. Confirm the value is stored correctly, visible to the right people, and usable in reports if required. Consider existing records before introducing a required field.

Verify and troubleshoot

If a field is missing, inspect field-level security, the assigned layout, and Dynamic Forms visibility. Removing a field from a layout does not secure it against API or report access.

Title: Configure Page Layouts and Lightning Record Pages
Summary: Arrange record fields and actions while understanding layout and record-page assignments.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Arrange record fields and actions while understanding layout and record-page assignments.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience with an administrator or delegated administrator who has permission to manage these settings. Test configuration changes in a development or test org first. Available options depend on edition, licenses, and enabled features.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager, select the object, and open Page Layouts. Clone an existing layout when a separate experience is needed, or edit the relevant layout.
  2. Arrange sections and fields, configure supported buttons and actions, and review related lists. Save the layout and check Page Layout Assignment for the applicable profile and record type.
  3. To change the broader Lightning record page, open the record and choose Edit Page, or use Lightning App Builder in Setup. Arrange components and review component visibility. Save and activate the page for the intended app, record type, or profiles.
  4. Test in the actual app with a representative user. On pages that use Dynamic Forms, field placement and visibility are configured on the Lightning page rather than solely through the Record Detail component.

Verify and troubleshoot

If users see an old page, check activation and assignments. Layout-level required fields guide the UI; use an appropriate field requirement or validation rule when enforcement must also apply to data loaded through APIs.

Title: Set Up Record Types and Picklist Values
Summary: Provide different business processes, picklist choices, and page layouts for an object.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Provide different business processes, picklist choices, and page layouts for an object.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience with an administrator or delegated administrator who has permission to manage these settings. Test configuration changes in a development or test org first. Available options depend on edition, licenses, and enabled features.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager, choose the object, and open Record Types. Before creating one, confirm that the requirement needs different processes or choices rather than only a different page appearance.
  2. Create a record type with a clear label and description. For objects that use a business process, select or create the appropriate process. Make the record type active and enable it for the relevant profiles.
  3. Configure the available picklist values and defaults for the record type. Assign page layouts for the relevant profile and record-type combinations.
  4. Check each target user's record-type availability and default. Permission sets can grant record-type availability; page-layout assignment is managed through profile and record-type combinations. Test creating and editing records for each process.

Verify and troubleshoot

If a picklist option is missing, check the field's active values, record-type values, and any controlling-field dependency. Record types do not establish record-level security.

Title: Configure Organization-Wide Defaults and Sharing
Summary: Establish baseline record visibility and extend access to the right users.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Establish baseline record visibility and extend access to the right users.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience with an administrator or delegated administrator who has permission to manage these settings. Test configuration changes in a development or test org first. Available options depend on edition, licenses, and enabled features.

Steps

  1. In Setup, search for Sharing Settings. Review the internal and, where available, external organization-wide defaults for the object. Choose a baseline such as Private or Public Read Only that matches the business requirement and supported object options.
  2. Review ownership and the role hierarchy. Hierarchy behavior depends on the object and configuration; a user's role is not the same as the user's profile.
  3. Where additional record access is needed, configure an appropriate owner-based or criteria-based sharing rule and target role or public group. Sharing rules open access beyond the baseline; they do not restrict access already available.
  4. Allow sharing recalculation to finish and verify access with test users who should and should not see sample records. Check object permissions and field-level security alongside sharing.

Verify and troubleshoot

If access is broader than expected, inspect ownership, hierarchy, teams, manual shares, sharing rules, and View All or Modify All permissions. Changing a list-view filter does not change record security.

Title: Create Validation Rules for Data Quality
Summary: Prevent invalid record values with a clear rule and an actionable error message.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Prevent invalid record values with a clear rule and an actionable error message.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience with an administrator or delegated administrator who has permission to manage these settings. Test configuration changes in a development or test org first. Available options depend on edition, licenses, and enabled features.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager, choose the object, and open Validation Rules. Select New and enter a descriptive rule name and business-focused description.
  2. Build a formula that evaluates to TRUE when the record should be rejected. Use the formula editor and Check Syntax. For example, a business rule can require an explanation when a particular status is selected.
  3. Enter an error message explaining what must be corrected and choose a useful error location. Save the rule and activate it when ready.
  4. Test both valid and invalid records, including updates to existing data. Review imports, integrations, and automation that write to the object, because validation rules can block those changes too. Avoid introducing a rule without considering existing records.

Verify and troubleshoot

If a save fails unexpectedly, inspect all active validation rules and the values produced by automation. A validation rule detects invalid data; it does not populate the missing value or automatically correct the record.

Title: Check Email Deliverability and Sender Settings
Summary: Review outbound email access and sender verification when Salesforce emails are missing.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Review outbound email access and sender verification when Salesforce emails are missing.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience with an administrator or delegated administrator who has permission to manage these settings. Test configuration changes in a development or test org first. Available options depend on edition, licenses, and enabled features.

Steps

  1. In Setup, search for Deliverability. Review the Access Level and select the setting appropriate for this environment. System email settings and All Email allow different categories of messages; do not assume a newly created test org permits every outbound message.
  2. Review Organization-Wide Addresses if users or automation need an approved shared sender. Add the address and complete the verification process before relying on it.
  3. Check the sending user's email verification and relevant organization domain-verification requirements. Review email relay or domain authentication configuration with the mail administrator when these are used.
  4. Send a controlled test using the same feature and sender as the real use case. Check the recipient's junk folder and request Salesforce Email Log Files when available to investigate delivery.

Verify and troubleshoot

If email still does not arrive, check feature-specific configuration, daily limits, recipient validity, and mail-server filtering. Enabling All Email does not guarantee delivery or override sender verification and platform limits.

Title: Create Reports and Dashboards
Summary: Build a basic report and dashboard, and share them with the appropriate audience.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Build a basic report and dashboard, and share them with the appropriate audience.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience with an administrator or delegated administrator who has permission to manage these settings. Test configuration changes in a development or test org first. Available options depend on edition, licenses, and enabled features.

Steps

  1. Open Reports from the App Launcher or navigation bar and select New Report. Choose a report type that includes the required objects and relationships.
  2. Add useful columns and filters. Check the date range and Show Me filter so the report returns the intended records. Group rows and add summaries when needed, then save the report in a suitable folder.
  3. Open Dashboards and select New Dashboard. Add a component using the saved report, choose a suitable chart or metric, and save the dashboard in an appropriate folder.
  4. Review report and dashboard folder sharing. Check the dashboard running user or dynamic-dashboard configuration, because it affects whose data is displayed. Refresh and test with the intended audience.

Verify and troubleshoot

If records are missing, inspect report filters, report-type relationships, object and field permissions, and sharing. Folder access lets someone open a report; it does not automatically grant access to every underlying record.

Title: Configure Business Hours for a Support Team
Summary: Define support working hours and time zones for features that use a business-hours schedule.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Define support working hours and time zones for features that use a business-hours schedule.

Before you begin

Agree the supported days, opening times, and regional time zone with the support manager. Use an administrator with permission to customize the organization.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Company settings can affect several teams and reporting processes. Confirm the configuration owner and intended audience before changing an organization-level default. When investigating a problem, inspect the current setting before assuming a new feature must be enabled.

Steps

  1. In Setup, enter Business Hours in Quick Find and open Business Hours. Review existing schedules before creating another one; a suitable schedule may already serve the team.
  2. Select New Business Hours or edit the relevant schedule. Enter a name that identifies the region or service and select its time zone rather than assuming the company default is appropriate.
  3. Enter each working day and its opening and closing times. Use the available all-day option only for genuine continuous coverage; leave nonworking days without a working interval.
  4. Save the schedule and make it active when ready. Mark it as default only if features using the organization default should adopt this schedule.
  5. Review the escalation rules or other supported service features that reference business hours. Associate the intended schedule in each feature; creating a schedule does not automatically assign it everywhere.
  6. Record the schedule owner and review date. Add associated holidays separately so an otherwise normal working day can be excluded from support-time calculations.

Example

A London team supports customers Monday through Friday during local office hours. Give that team a London-based schedule instead of copying a New York schedule and manually shifting the clock times.

Verify the result

Test a supported escalation or business-time calculation during an open interval, outside opening hours, and over a weekend. Check the schedule time zone and confirm the consuming feature references the expected schedule.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If time appears to pass incorrectly, inspect the consuming feature, default schedule, time zone, and associated holidays. User display time zones can make an escalation timestamp appear different without changing the underlying scheduled instant.

Limitations

Business hours supply calendars to supported features. They do not prevent users from signing in, block record creation, or establish a contractual service entitlement by themselves.

Title: Add Holidays to Business-Hours Schedules
Summary: Exclude full days or partial closures from the working calendars used by support features.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Exclude full days or partial closures from the working calendars used by support features.

Before you begin

Have an existing business-hours schedule and an approved holiday calendar. Determine whether each closure is a full day, a partial day, or a recurring event.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Company settings can affect several teams and reporting processes. Confirm the configuration owner and intended audience before changing an organization-level default. When investigating a problem, inspect the current setting before assuming a new feature must be enabled.

Steps

  1. In Setup, find Holidays. Review existing entries to avoid creating multiple holidays that describe the same closure for the same support team.
  2. Select New and enter a clear name and description. Set the date and choose the full-day option or enter the start and end times for a partial closure.
  3. If recurrence is needed and supported by the form, configure the recurrence pattern and end date. Check that the pattern matches the actual observed holiday rather than only its usual calendar date.
  4. Save the holiday, then associate it with the appropriate business-hours schedules through the available Business Hours related list or schedule association controls.
  5. Review each association carefully when teams work in different regions. A holiday for one support center should not automatically close every schedule in the organization.
  6. Test the consuming service feature and document who will maintain next year's calendar. Add exceptional closures explicitly when the recurring pattern does not cover them.

Example

For a support center closing at noon on a particular Friday, create a partial-day holiday covering the closure interval and associate it only with that center's business hours.

Verify the result

Open the saved holiday and confirm its dates, recurrence, and business-hours associations. Run a supported timing scenario across the closure and confirm that only working intervals contribute to elapsed business time.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a closure is ignored, check the association to the exact schedule used by the feature. If too much time is excluded, look for overlapping holidays, a full-day selection, or an unintended recurrence range.

Limitations

A holiday is not a company-wide login restriction. Regional time-zone and feature behavior still matter; verify partial-day closures against the schedule that actually consumes them.

Title: Configure a Standard Fiscal Year
Summary: Align fiscal reporting periods with a business year that starts in a month other than January.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Align fiscal reporting periods with a business year that starts in a month other than January.

Before you begin

Obtain finance approval for the start month and fiscal-year naming convention. Inventory forecasts, quotas, reports, and integrations that depend on fiscal periods before changing the setting.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Company settings can affect several teams and reporting processes. Confirm the configuration owner and intended audience before changing an organization-level default. When investigating a problem, inspect the current setting before assuming a new feature must be enabled.

Steps

  1. In Setup, search for Fiscal Year. Read the current configuration and determine whether the org uses standard fiscal years or has already enabled custom fiscal years.
  2. For a standard fiscal year, choose Edit and select the month in which the fiscal year begins. Standard fiscal years retain calendar-month boundaries even when the first month changes.
  3. Choose whether the fiscal-year name follows the year in which the period begins or ends. Confirm the interpretation with finance using a concrete start and end date.
  4. Review the page warnings before saving. Fiscal-period changes can affect forecast-related data, including quotas and adjustments, so capture the relevant baseline beforehand.
  5. Save only after testing the proposed configuration in a suitable test environment. Update saved reports that use explicit calendar dates when they should instead use fiscal-period filters.
  6. Compare fiscal-quarter and fiscal-year reports with the approved finance calendar. Communicate the reporting change and the date it becomes effective to report owners.

Example

If the business year runs from April through March, finance must decide whether April 2026 through March 2027 is named FY2026 or FY2027 before users interpret fiscal filters.

Verify the result

Run a report containing records on both sides of the fiscal-year boundary. Confirm the fiscal grouping and relative date filters place each record in the intended quarter and year.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a report remains on calendar periods, check its grouping and date filter rather than changing the fiscal year again. Investigate custom fiscal-year configuration separately if standard controls are unavailable.

Limitations

Do not enable custom fiscal years merely to change a start month. Custom fiscal years are a separate, consequential configuration and require their own design and impact review.

Title: Set User Language, Locale, and Time Zone
Summary: Correct an individual user's date, number, language, and time display without changing company defaults.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Correct an individual user's date, number, language, and time display without changing company defaults.

Before you begin

Ask which display is wrong and obtain a concrete example. Distinguish interface language, regional formatting, and time zone; each setting solves a different problem.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Company settings can affect several teams and reporting processes. Confirm the configuration owner and intended audience before changing an organization-level default. When investigating a problem, inspect the current setting before assuming a new feature must be enabled.

Steps

  1. For your own account, open your avatar and Settings, then find Language & Time Zone under personal information. Administrators can review the corresponding fields on a user record in Setup.
  2. Choose the user's language from the enabled options. This controls supported interface translations; it does not automatically translate business data or custom text that lacks a translation.
  3. Set Locale to the region whose date and number formats the user expects. Check an ambiguous date and a decimal amount before choosing between similarly named locales.
  4. Set Time Zone to the user's working region. Select the appropriate regional zone so daylight-saving adjustments follow that zone instead of relying on a manually calculated offset.
  5. Save and refresh the session as needed. Compare a known Date/Time value with another user in a different region while checking that both refer to the same event.
  6. Review calendar integrations and export/import formats separately if the problem occurs outside the Salesforce interface. Record the expected external format rather than assuming personal settings govern every integration.

Example

Two colleagues can see the same meeting at different local times. Changing one person's time zone should correct their display without editing the meeting's stored instant or the other person's settings.

Verify the result

Check a record with a Date field, a Date/Time field, and a decimal value. Confirm the interface language and formatting are appropriate and the event corresponds to the intended local time.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a custom component still displays a fixed format, ask its owner how formatting is implemented. If only imported values are wrong, inspect the source time zone and import mapping before changing user settings again.

Limitations

Date-only values represent calendar dates, not instants to shift across time zones. Available languages depend on org configuration, and personal settings do not translate article content.

Title: Review Setup Changes with Setup Audit Trail
Summary: Investigate who changed supported administrative settings and when those changes occurred.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Investigate who changed supported administrative settings and when those changes occurred.

Before you begin

Use an administrator or another user authorized to view setup history. Collect the approximate change time, affected feature, and suspected setting before investigating.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Company settings can affect several teams and reporting processes. Confirm the configuration owner and intended audience before changing an organization-level default. When investigating a problem, inspect the current setting before assuming a new feature must be enabled.

Steps

  1. In Setup, enter View Setup Audit Trail in Quick Find and open the audit-trail page. Review the recent entries displayed on the page.
  2. Look for the date, user, action, and section associated with the suspected configuration. Compare the time with the reported incident and account for the time zone used in the display.
  3. Download the available setup audit history when a wider time window or offline filtering is needed. Save the download in an approved location because administrative activity can contain sensitive operational information.
  4. Filter for the relevant feature or administrator and compare related changes in sequence. A single user request can lead to several entries, so avoid treating the first match as the entire change.
  5. Compare the current setting with your approved baseline or deployment record. Audit history helps identify a change but does not supply a complete restorable metadata backup.
  6. Record the relevant entry details and investigate with the change owner. If a correction is required, test the specific setting change and follow the normal configuration-change process.

Example

When users lose a previously available setup capability, search the relevant window for profile or permission changes and correlate the entries with deployments and planned administration work.

Verify the result

Make a harmless, approved configuration change in a test org and confirm a corresponding supported entry appears. Confirm the downloaded history covers the period needed for your investigation.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If there is no matching entry, verify the time window and whether the action is captured by Setup Audit Trail. Use record field history, login history, deployment results, or other logs for different kinds of events.

Limitations

Setup Audit Trail tracks supported configuration changes rather than every user action. Its retention is limited; archive required history according to your organization's retention process.

Title: Monitor Data and File Storage Usage
Summary: Identify storage pressure and plan targeted cleanup without confusing record storage with file storage.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Identify storage pressure and plan targeted cleanup without confusing record storage with file storage.

Before you begin

Use an administrator with access to storage information. Agree retention requirements with data owners before proposing deletion, and identify the org whose capacity is being reviewed.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Company settings can affect several teams and reporting processes. Confirm the configuration owner and intended audience before changing an organization-level default. When investigating a problem, inspect the current setting before assuming a new feature must be enabled.

Steps

  1. In Setup, search for Storage Usage and open the page. Note the organization's limits and used amounts for data storage and file storage separately.
  2. Review the object-level data-storage breakdown. Identify which objects consume the most capacity and compare those findings with expected business growth rather than judging only by record count.
  3. Review available file-storage details and ownership information. Large or duplicated files can create a different problem from many small business records.
  4. Compare current usage with a previous measurement and establish a review interval. Record the date because reported storage figures may not reflect every recent change immediately.
  5. Ask each data owner whether old records or files can be archived, reduced, or removed. Confirm relationships, integrations, legal retention, and recovery requirements before choosing a cleanup method.
  6. After an approved pilot cleanup or capacity change, recheck usage when calculations update. Keep the result and the cleanup scope so the next review can distinguish growth from reporting delay.

Example

A sales org with ample data storage can still approach its file limit because users upload large presentations. Deleting unrelated contact records would not address that file-storage problem.

Verify the result

Confirm you can identify the dominant storage category and its largest contributors. After any separately approved cleanup, reconcile the exact deleted items and check usage again after the platform recalculates it.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If usage does not fall immediately, consider reporting delay and the lifecycle of deleted content. Check the actual storage category and file versions before assuming the deletion failed or repeating a destructive operation.

Limitations

Storage Usage is a capacity view, not a backup or retention policy. Do not delete business data solely to improve a percentage; choose an approved archive or capacity strategy.

Title: Review User Licenses and Feature Entitlements
Summary: Check license availability and distinguish user licenses from permission set licenses and package licenses.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Check license availability and distinguish user licenses from permission set licenses and package licenses.

Before you begin

List the capabilities the user needs and the relevant product names. Use an administrator who can review users, licenses, and installed packages.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Company settings can affect several teams and reporting processes. Confirm the configuration owner and intended audience before changing an organization-level default. When investigating a problem, inspect the current setting before assuming a new feature must be enabled.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Company Information and review the available, used, and remaining user-license counts. Confirm that you are checking the correct org and environment.
  2. Open the affected user record and inspect the assigned user license and compatible profile. A user license defines a capability boundary rather than granting every permission within that boundary.
  3. Review Permission Set License Assignments when the product requires an additional entitlement. Check availability before attempting to grant a permission set that depends on that license.
  4. For an installed managed package, inspect its licensing page in Installed Packages when applicable. Package access can require a package license in addition to the user's ordinary permissions.
  5. Compare the user with a functioning user who has the same job, but grant only the entitlements and permissions required for the intended task. Avoid copying unrelated privileged access.
  6. Recheck counts after any separately approved assignment or deactivation. Document the product entitlement owner so future access requests reach the right administrator.

Example

A permission set assignment can fail even though the user is active and has a Salesforce license. The permission set may require a separate permission set license that has no available seats.

Verify the result

Confirm the expected entitlement is available and associated with the correct user. Test the actual feature using a representative account after permissions are configured, rather than relying only on the presence of a license.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the feature remains absent, distinguish license compatibility, permission assignments, application visibility, and feature enablement. If counts differ from a purchase record, contact the subscription owner rather than assuming licenses transfer automatically between orgs.

Limitations

A license is not a substitute for object, field, record, or feature permissions. Product availability varies by edition and contract, so treat the org's actual entitlements as authoritative.

Title: Rename Standard Tabs and Field Labels
Summary: Use business-friendly labels while preserving the distinction between display names and API names.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Use business-friendly labels while preserving the distinction between display names and API names.

Before you begin

Agree the new terminology with business owners and integration maintainers. Identify whether the label belongs to a standard tab, a standard field, or a custom field before choosing the editing tool.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Company settings can affect several teams and reporting processes. Confirm the configuration owner and intended audience before changing an organization-level default. When investigating a problem, inspect the current setting before assuming a new feature must be enabled.

Steps

  1. In Setup, find Rename Tabs and Labels for supported standard objects. Locate the object whose displayed name should match the business vocabulary.
  2. Review the singular and plural labels and follow the editing wizard for any supported standard field labels. Use names that remain clear in lists, record pages, and reports.
  3. For a custom field, use Object Manager, select the object, and edit the field's label in Fields & Relationships. Keep an existing API name stable unless a separate technical change has been designed.
  4. Review translations when the org supports more than one language. A default-language rename does not guarantee that every translated interface will show the intended wording.
  5. Save and review the object navigation, a record page, and a report using the renamed field. Check help text and training material for terms that now need updating.
  6. Tell report authors and support staff both the display label and underlying API name. That mapping helps users recognize a field whose technical identifier has not changed.

Example

A team can display Accounts using an approved customer-oriented label while integrations continue to address the Account object. The renamed screen text does not create a new object or migrate existing records.

Verify the result

Open the relevant app and confirm singular and plural names read naturally. Check a report column and a field-selection dialog, then verify that the original API name remains available to integrations.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a label is unchanged in one location, check whether the component uses custom text or a translation. If an integration fails, investigate a separate API-name edit rather than assuming a display-label change should break its mapping.

Limitations

Only supported standard labels can be renamed through this feature. Renaming a label does not change security, ownership, data type, or business behavior associated with the object.

Title: Use Schema Builder to Review Object Relationships
Summary: Inspect an object model visually before adding fields or changing relationships.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Inspect an object model visually before adding fields or changing relationships.

Before you begin

Use an administrator or a user with the permissions needed to inspect the schema. Identify the business process and relevant standard and custom objects before opening the diagram.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Company settings can affect several teams and reporting processes. Confirm the configuration owner and intended audience before changing an organization-level default. When investigating a problem, inspect the current setting before assuming a new feature must be enabled.

Steps

  1. In Setup, search for Schema Builder and open it. Use the object list to select the small set of objects relevant to the process rather than displaying the entire org at once.
  2. Locate the objects and review their fields and relationship lines. Read each relationship's details to distinguish a lookup from a master-detail relationship and identify the child object that stores the reference.
  3. Compare the model with an actual record journey, such as a child record belonging to a parent. Record which object owns the business fact before proposing a new field.
  4. Open Object Manager for details that need closer inspection, including field-level security, requiredness, sharing settings, and page layouts. A diagram alone does not establish the full access model.
  5. Document missing or redundant relationships and check reports, flows, imports, and integrations that use them. Review destructive implications before considering any relationship conversion or deletion.
  6. Save the findings as a design note or screenshot according to your team's process. If creation controls are available in Schema Builder, leave them unused during a review-only exercise.

Example

Before adding an account name as free text to a custom request, inspect whether the request already has an Account lookup. An existing relationship may satisfy reporting needs without duplicating the account's name.

Verify the result

Confirm the diagram includes the relevant parent and child objects and that relationship types match Object Manager. Trace at least one real sample record through the relationships you documented.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If an expected object is missing, check selection filters, object availability, and your permissions. If records are inaccessible, inspect object permissions and record sharing separately; a visible schema relationship does not grant data access.

Limitations

Schema Builder describes structure rather than complete automation or security behavior. Creating or changing fields from the diagram is a real configuration change and should follow the same review process as Object Manager.

Title: Freeze and Unfreeze a Salesforce User
Summary: Temporarily prevent a user from logging in while keeping the user account active.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Temporarily prevent a user from logging in while keeping the user account active.

Before you begin

Identify the exact user and reason for the temporary restriction. Use an administrator with user-management access and coordinate with your security team when handling an incident.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Keep user identity, authentication, and business permissions separate during troubleshooting. Use a dedicated test account for access checks and an independent administrator recovery route for restrictive login changes. Do not record passwords, recovery links, or verification codes in support notes.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Users and select the affected user by username. Confirm the account belongs to the intended person and environment before changing login access.
  2. On the user detail page, select Freeze when that action is available. Read the resulting state to confirm the login restriction was applied.
  3. Leave the account active if the purpose is a temporary hold. Review ongoing record ownership and automation dependencies while a permanent offboarding decision is being prepared.
  4. If the restriction is incident-related, review active sessions and connected application access through the appropriate controls. Do not assume that freezing is a complete response to every existing credential or integration risk.
  5. Document the reason, owner, and intended review date. Tell the support team that a frozen account differs from an account that has been deactivated or locked after password failures.
  6. When the restriction is approved for removal, return to the same user and select Unfreeze. Test the normal login route and any remaining authentication requirements.

Example

A departing employee can be frozen while administrators resolve ownership and workflow dependencies that temporarily block deactivation. Freezing prevents new login without completing the entire offboarding process.

Verify the result

Confirm the detail page shows the frozen state and the user cannot start an ordinary login. After unfreezing, verify that the user can authenticate through the approved route and still has the intended access.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the user still cannot log in after unfreezing, check activation, password lockout, MFA, SSO, login hours, and IP restrictions. These are separate controls and are not all reset by the Unfreeze action.

Limitations

Freezing does not deactivate the user or release their user license. It does not transfer owned records, remove permission assignments, or replace an incident-specific review of sessions and tokens.

Title: Deactivate a Departing User Safely
Summary: Remove a user's active access after reviewing ownership, automation, and operational dependencies.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Remove a user's active access after reviewing ownership, automation, and operational dependencies.

Before you begin

Obtain the approved offboarding time and identify a replacement owner. Use a user administrator and coordinate separately with the identity-provider and integration owners when applicable.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Keep user identity, authentication, and business permissions separate during troubleshooting. Use a dedicated test account for access checks and an independent administrator recovery route for restrictive login changes. Do not record passwords, recovery links, or verification codes in support notes.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Users and inspect the departing user's account. If access must stop immediately while dependencies are investigated, consider the Freeze action as a temporary measure.
  2. Inventory owned records, queue and group memberships, report subscriptions, dashboard running-user references, and automation settings that depend on the user. Identify service accounts before deactivating a seemingly unused login.
  3. Transfer responsibilities through the supported tools for each record or feature. Confirm whether related records require their own transfers instead of assuming every child follows the parent owner.
  4. Edit the user and clear Active. If Salesforce blocks deactivation, read the named dependency and replace the user in that configuration rather than repeatedly saving the same change.
  5. Save and verify the inactive state. Review external identity-provider access, connected applications, notification recipients, and delegated administration as part of the agreed offboarding process.
  6. Retain an offboarding record identifying ownership changes, remaining historical references, and any follow-up work. Check license availability separately after deactivation.

Example

Before deactivating a sales manager, replace that manager as the running user of shared dashboards and transfer open opportunities to the approved successor. Historical Created By references should remain attributable to the original user.

Verify the result

Confirm the account is inactive, ordinary login is blocked, and the successor can perform the transferred tasks. Check that reports, scheduled processes, and notification routes continue to work without the departed user.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If deactivation is blocked, inspect the specific error for default ownership or automation references. If a process fails afterward, compare its running user and ownership assumptions with the offboarding inventory.

Limitations

Users are deactivated rather than deleted. Deactivation does not automatically transfer records or prove that all external sessions, credentials, and integrations have been handled.

Title: Reset a Password and Unlock a User
Summary: Distinguish a forgotten password from password lockout and help the user recover through the correct route.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Distinguish a forgotten password from password lockout and help the user recover through the correct route.

Before you begin

Verify the requester's identity using your support process. Determine whether the user signs in with a Salesforce password or through an external identity provider.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Keep user identity, authentication, and business permissions separate during troubleshooting. Use a dedicated test account for access checks and an independent administrator recovery route for restrictive login changes. Do not record passwords, recovery links, or verification codes in support notes.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Users and locate the account by username. Check that it is active and not frozen before treating the issue as a password problem.
  2. Review the available lockout indication on the user detail page and use Unlock when the account is locked and that action is available. Unlocking does not require changing the password in every case.
  3. For a local Salesforce password reset, use Reset Password for the confirmed user. Check the registered email address and notify the user to follow the Salesforce reset instructions privately.
  4. For SSO credentials, direct the user to the approved identity-provider recovery procedure. Resetting a local Salesforce password does not change an identity-provider password.
  5. Ask the user to complete a fresh login through the correct org route and satisfy any MFA challenge. Do not request their password, recovery link, or verification code.
  6. Review Login History if the new attempt fails. Record the failure category and timestamp so that the next investigation targets the actual authentication control.

Example

A user who repeatedly entered an old password may need an unlock and a password reset. A user whose SSO account is disabled needs identity-provider assistance even if Salesforce shows the account as active.

Verify the result

Confirm the reset message reaches the registered recipient and the user can complete a new login. Check that any unlock status has cleared and the successful attempt appears in Login History.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If no reset email arrives, inspect email validity, delivery restrictions, and spam filtering. If authentication still fails, check frozen state, login hours, IP restrictions, SSO routing, and MFA rather than repeatedly resetting the password.

Limitations

Password recovery and MFA recovery are different workflows. Session termination on an administrator reset depends on security settings; verify your org policy instead of assuming every session is ended.

Title: Investigate Failed Logins with Login History
Summary: Use login status, time, and source information to narrow down an authentication failure.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Use login status, time, and source information to narrow down an authentication failure.

Before you begin

Collect the username, approximate failure time, login method, and exact user-visible message. Use an administrator authorized to inspect login information.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Keep user identity, authentication, and business permissions separate during troubleshooting. Use a dedicated test account for access checks and an independent administrator recovery route for restrictive login changes. Do not record passwords, recovery links, or verification codes in support notes.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Login History for the organization, or inspect Login History from the affected user's detail page when available. Confirm you are examining the correct account.
  2. Find the attempt near the reported time and read its status, application or login type, source IP, and other available details. Align timestamps before correlating them with external logs.
  3. Separate invalid-credential failures from policy restrictions and identity-provider errors. The observed category determines whether to investigate password recovery, network restrictions, activation, or SSO.
  4. Compare a failed attempt with a successful attempt from the same approved login route. Differences in application, IP address, or authentication method can explain inconsistent results.
  5. Download the available history when a wider investigation requires filtering or correlation. Store it in an approved location because it contains user and network information.
  6. Ask the user to make one controlled attempt after the relevant correction. Check the new result and document the cause rather than applying several unrelated security changes at once.

Example

If a user logs in successfully from the office but fails from home, compare the source addresses and status before changing their password. Profile login IP restrictions may explain the difference.

Verify the result

Locate the controlled retry and verify that its status matches the user's experience. If it succeeds, confirm the intended application opens and the issue is resolved through the normal login path.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If no entry appears, verify the org URL, account, timestamp, and whether the request reached Salesforce. For SSO failures, correlate identity-provider logs because some failures occur before Salesforce receives a complete login.

Limitations

Login History is an authentication investigation tool, not a record of every subsequent page view. A successful login also does not prove the user has permission to perform a particular business task.

Title: Set Profile Login Hours
Summary: Restrict when users assigned to a profile can log in according to an approved access schedule.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Restrict when users assigned to a profile can log in according to an approved access schedule.

Before you begin

Obtain the approved days, time window, and time-zone interpretation. Identify every user sharing the profile and arrange a recovery path before testing a restrictive configuration.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Keep user identity, authentication, and business permissions separate during troubleshooting. Use a dedicated test account for access checks and an independent administrator recovery route for restrictive login changes. Do not record passwords, recovery links, or verification codes in support notes.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Profiles and select the profile that applies to the intended users. Review its assigned users so a schedule change does not unexpectedly affect another team.
  2. Open Login Hours and edit the allowed intervals for each day. Read the time-zone information shown on the configuration page rather than assuming each user's personal time zone controls the restriction.
  3. Define weekdays, weekends, and exceptions according to the approved policy. Check how the form represents a fully blocked day and a full day of allowed access before saving.
  4. Test the proposed schedule in a test org with a representative user. Include an attempt just inside the allowed period and another outside it, while retaining independent administrator access.
  5. Save the approved configuration and communicate the schedule, time zone, and support procedure. Review remote teams and seasonal working patterns before adopting one shared profile schedule.
  6. Recheck the behavior of an already logged-in test session at the boundary. Document the observed session behavior so support staff do not promise instant logout without verification.

Example

A team working in one region may require weekday access during local business hours. A shared profile used by a second region needs a deliberate policy decision before the same window is imposed.

Verify the result

Use controlled logins inside and outside the permitted window and inspect Login History. Verify that the restriction affects the intended profile population and leaves the administrator recovery route available.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a valid user is blocked at an unexpected time, inspect the profile's configured schedule and displayed time zone. Distinguish login-hour failures from password lockouts and network restrictions using Login History.

Limitations

Login hours are a profile-level authentication control. Business Hours schedules do not enforce them, and an organization's support calendar is not a substitute for a login policy.

Title: Distinguish Trusted IP Ranges from Login IP Restrictions
Summary: Choose the appropriate network setting without confusing identity-verification trust with an access allowlist.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Choose the appropriate network setting without confusing identity-verification trust with an access allowlist.

Before you begin

Obtain approved public network ranges from the network team. Include VPN and remote-work scenarios and preserve a separate administrator recovery route.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Keep user identity, authentication, and business permissions separate during troubleshooting. Use a dedicated test account for access checks and an independent administrator recovery route for restrictive login changes. Do not record passwords, recovery links, or verification codes in support notes.

Steps

  1. In Setup, review Network Access to see organization-level trusted IP ranges. These ranges relate to verification behavior and are different from a profile's Login IP Ranges.
  2. Open the target profile and inspect Login IP Ranges. A configured profile range restricts login to the permitted addresses, so inventory all users assigned to that profile.
  3. Translate the network team's approved ranges into the start and end addresses required by the page. Do not enter a private workstation address when Salesforce sees a shared public egress address.
  4. Test the proposed configuration in a test org from an allowed network and a disallowed network. Keep another administrator session and recovery route available during the test.
  5. Review session settings that may enforce login IP ranges on every request. Document the actual policy because checking only the initial login may not describe subsequent session behavior.
  6. Save only the approved settings and tell users how to connect through the supported network route. Inspect Login History after a controlled attempt to verify the source address Salesforce recorded.

Example

Adding the office public address as a trusted range does not by itself block a home login. A profile Login IP Range is the separate control used when policy requires an address-based restriction.

Verify the result

Confirm the allowed source succeeds and the restricted source fails for the intended reason. Check the recorded source IP and repeat through the approved VPN route when that is part of normal access.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If users are unexpectedly blocked, verify public egress addresses, VPN routing, profile assignment, and session enforcement settings. Avoid widening a range to every address as a permanent troubleshooting shortcut.

Limitations

Trusted networks do not waive MFA requirements. Network controls complement authentication and permissions; they do not grant access to objects, fields, records, or applications.

Title: Enroll a User in Multi-Factor Authentication
Summary: Help a user register an approved verification method for Salesforce interface authentication.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Help a user register an approved verification method for Salesforce interface authentication.

Before you begin

Confirm the organization's MFA policy, supported methods, and direct-login or SSO route. Use a separate test user and retain an approved recovery method before changing authentication enforcement.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Keep user identity, authentication, and business permissions separate during troubleshooting. Use a dedicated test account for access checks and an independent administrator recovery route for restrictive login changes. Do not record passwords, recovery links, or verification codes in support notes.

Steps

  1. Review the organization's authentication configuration and determine where MFA is enforced. For SSO, coordinate with the identity team rather than assuming the direct Salesforce login setting governs every route.
  2. Confirm the user is included in the approved enforcement policy or applicable permission assignment. Do not add exemptions merely to avoid the enrollment process.
  3. Ask the user to start a fresh login through their normal route. Follow the presented registration process for an organization-approved method such as Salesforce Authenticator or a supported security key.
  4. Have the user complete the method association and a verification challenge themselves. Administrators should not ask users to send verification codes or approve an unexplained authentication request.
  5. Record the recovery procedure and help the user register a permitted backup method when the organization supports one. Explain how to recognize and reject an unexpected verification prompt.
  6. Test another sign-in and confirm the challenge is completed with the enrolled method. Update onboarding guidance to identify who handles device changes and lost-method recovery.

Example

A new employee can associate Salesforce Authenticator during onboarding and verify a second login before leaving the session. This identifies enrollment problems while support and the user are both available.

Verify the result

Confirm the user can sign out and authenticate again using the approved method. Check the registered-method details available to administrators and ensure the recovery process is understood.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If enrollment does not appear, inspect the route, existing methods, and enforcement policy. If the challenge fails, check device connectivity and method-specific requirements before removing or resetting any registered factor.

Limitations

Approved methods and enforcement options vary by organization and release. MFA enrollment does not grant business permissions, and a password reset alone does not replace MFA recovery.

Title: Recover Access After an MFA Device Is Lost
Summary: Restore a verified user's authentication method using the organization's approved recovery process.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Restore a verified user's authentication method using the organization's approved recovery process.

Before you begin

Verify identity using the security team's recovery procedure. Determine whether the lost method is managed by Salesforce or by the organization's identity provider.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Keep user identity, authentication, and business permissions separate during troubleshooting. Use a dedicated test account for access checks and an independent administrator recovery route for restrictive login changes. Do not record passwords, recovery links, or verification codes in support notes.

Steps

  1. Ask the verified user whether an approved backup verification method is available. If so, have the user sign in with that method rather than removing a working factor unnecessarily.
  2. For Salesforce-managed methods, open the user's detail page in Setup and review registered verification methods and available recovery controls. Choose the action for the specific lost method.
  3. Disconnect or reset only the affected registration according to policy. If a temporary verification code is available and authorized, treat it as a short-lived secret and follow the organization's delivery procedure.
  4. Have the user enroll a replacement method through a controlled login and complete a challenge. For identity-provider MFA, use that provider's recovery workflow with the identity team instead.
  5. Review unexpected login activity when a device may have been stolen. Coordinate session and credential actions with security rather than assuming factor replacement resolves a potential compromise.
  6. Confirm a new sign-in works, retire temporary recovery material, and document the recovery event without storing verification secrets. Encourage an approved backup method for future incidents.

Example

A user with a lost phone but a registered security key can authenticate with the key, replace the phone association, and confirm the new phone works before discarding temporary recovery options.

Verify the result

Verify that the replacement method succeeds on a fresh login and the lost method is no longer registered where applicable. Confirm the user follows the intended direct-login or SSO route.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the user still cannot log in, inspect account activation, frozen state, login restrictions, and whether the MFA challenge belongs to the identity provider. Avoid repeated password resets when the failure concerns a missing verification factor.

Limitations

Recovery actions require strong identity verification and appropriate administrative permissions. Do not solve lost-device recovery by permanently exempting the user from the organization's MFA policy.

Title: Test Configuration with a Representative User
Summary: Validate a business task using the permissions and assignments of the intended audience.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Validate a business task using the permissions and assignments of the intended audience.

Before you begin

Identify a test user with the target license, profile, permission sets, role, and record ownership. Use synthetic test records and obtain any required login-access authorization.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Keep user identity, authentication, and business permissions separate during troubleshooting. Use a dedicated test account for access checks and an independent administrator recovery route for restrictive login changes. Do not record passwords, recovery links, or verification codes in support notes.

Steps

  1. Define the task and expected result, including at least one action the user should not be allowed to perform. Record the relevant app, record type, and sample record.
  2. In Setup, review the test user's actual assignments. A system administrator is usually unsuitable for proving that a restricted business role has the correct access.
  3. If an approved Login action is available on the user detail page, use it according to the org's login-access policy. Otherwise ask the test user to perform the scenario in their own session.
  4. Open the intended app and run the full task, including creating or editing data where required. Check field visibility, action availability, record access, and the saved result.
  5. Repeat the negative scenario with a record or action outside the user's intended access. Do not treat a hidden button as proof that API or record access is restricted.
  6. End the impersonated session through the appropriate logout control and record the outcome. Make any further permission changes narrowly and rerun the failed scenario.

Example

When adding a field for support staff, test that a support user can read it on the correct case page and that an unrelated user cannot retrieve protected data through another available surface.

Verify the result

Confirm both the allowed task and the denied task match the access requirement. Check the exact user and record IDs used so the result can be reproduced after later changes.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If Login is unavailable, inspect the organization's administrator login policy and the user's granted login access. If the page differs, inspect app, profile, record-type, and Lightning page assignments before changing unrelated permissions.

Limitations

Impersonation can create real records and side effects. It is not a harmless visual preview, and it does not replace separate testing of integrations or automated execution contexts.

Title: Bundle Job Permissions with a Permission Set Group
Summary: Combine reusable permission sets into a role-oriented bundle and verify its calculated access.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Combine reusable permission sets into a role-oriented bundle and verify its calculated access.

Before you begin

Identify a specific job function and existing permission sets that support it. Check user-license and permission-set-license compatibility before choosing the group's members.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Evaluate object permissions, field permissions, and record access as separate layers. Use a test user whose other grants are understood, including group membership and broad administrative access. A successful administrator test is insufficient evidence for a restricted business role.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Permission Set Groups and select New. Enter a job-focused label and description explaining who should receive the bundle and what work it supports.
  2. Open the group and use Permission Sets in Group to add the required permission sets. Prefer small reusable permission sets rather than reproducing an entire administrator profile.
  3. Review the combined permissions and any sensitive object or system access. A group accumulates permissions from its members unless supported permissions are muted within that group.
  4. Check the group's calculation status and wait for it to become Updated. If the group is Outdated, use the available recalculation action and investigate a Failed state before assignment.
  5. Use Manage Assignments to assign the group to an approved test user. Check any license prerequisites reported by the assignment process instead of granting a broader license without review.
  6. Test the complete job and an excluded task. Document the group owner and review assignments when the user changes responsibilities or one of the underlying permission sets changes.

Example

A support onboarding group can combine case-editing, report-reading, and Knowledge-reading permission sets. Updating one reusable set changes the calculated group, so the impact extends beyond a single new user.

Verify the result

Confirm the calculation status is Updated and the test user has the expected group assignment. Verify object, field, and system access through real tasks and check record sharing separately.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If assignment fails, inspect license compatibility and permission dependencies. If access is unexpectedly broad, inspect the profile, individual permission sets, and other groups; they can grant access outside this bundle.

Limitations

Permission set groups do not create roles or automatically share records. Removing one group does not revoke permissions that remain available through another assignment.

Title: Mute Permissions Within a Permission Set Group
Summary: Suppress selected grants inside one permission set group without editing its reusable member sets.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Suppress selected grants inside one permission set group without editing its reusable member sets.

Before you begin

Have an existing permission set group and a precise list of permissions to suppress. Review all other grants to the test user before relying on a muted result.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Evaluate object permissions, field permissions, and record access as separate layers. Use a test user whose other grants are understood, including group membership and broad administrative access. A successful administrator test is insufficient evidence for a restricted business role.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Permission Set Groups and select the target group. Review its member permission sets and the permissions that should remain available to the job.
  2. Open Muting Permission Set in Group and create or edit the group's muting permission set through the available controls. Give it a description tied to the group's intended responsibilities.
