  3. Select supported object, field, or system permissions to mute. Read dependency messages carefully because muting a parent capability can affect dependent permissions within the group.
  4. Save and allow group recalculation to complete. Check that the group status returns to Updated before testing effective access.
  5. Assign the group to a controlled test user whose other grants are understood. Test both the muted action and an ordinary action that should still work.
  6. Compare that user with a second user who receives the original permission set directly. Document that the muting applies to the group calculation rather than changing the reusable permission set itself.

Example

A reusable Account permission set may include Delete, while a support group should exclude it. Muting Delete in that group does not remove Delete from another user assigned the original permission set directly.

Verify the result

Confirm the intended permission is suppressed for a user whose only relevant grant comes from the group. Verify the same permission remains available when legitimately granted through an independent assignment.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the action is still allowed, inspect the profile, other permission sets, other groups, and broad administrative permissions. Check recalculation status before assuming the muting configuration was ignored.

Limitations

Muting is not an organization-wide deny rule. It cannot cancel access independently granted by the profile or another permission assignment outside the affected group.

Title: Secure a Sensitive Field with Field-Level Security
Summary: Control whether users can read or edit a field independently of its position on a record page.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Control whether users can read or edit a field independently of its position on a record page.

Before you begin

Identify the object, field API name, approved reader population, and approved editor population. Distinguish data sensitivity from a preference to simplify the page.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Evaluate object permissions, field permissions, and record access as separate layers. Use a test user whose other grants are understood, including group membership and broad administrative access. A successful administrator test is insufficient evidence for a restricted business role.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager, select the object, and locate the field in Fields & Relationships. Review its existing field-level security and the permission sources that currently grant access.
  2. In the appropriate permission set, open Object Settings and the object's field permissions. Grant Read Access to approved readers and Edit Access only to approved editors.
  3. Review profiles and other permission sets for overlapping grants. Salesforce permissions are additive, so reducing one grant will not remove a permission supplied elsewhere.
  4. Review page layouts and Dynamic Forms placement separately. Put the field where approved users need it, but do not rely on hiding it from a layout as the access restriction.
  5. Test a reader, an editor, and a user who should have no access. Include record pages, reports, and a supported API-based check where appropriate to the application.
  6. Review formulas, reports, exports, and automation that might expose derived or copied sensitive data. Document the access model and the business owner who approves changes.

Example

A support user may need to read a customer reference number without editing it, while an integration-maintenance user can update it. Both users still need the appropriate object and record access.

Verify the result

Confirm read-only users cannot edit the field and unauthorized users cannot retrieve it through supported user-context surfaces. Verify authorized editors can save a valid value on a record they can edit.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the field is missing for an approved reader, inspect field permissions and page placement separately. If access remains too broad, trace all grants, including View All Fields where available, and examine formulas or copied fields that disclose the same information.

Limitations

Field-level security does not grant record access. System-context automation and custom code can have different enforcement behavior and need their own security review.

Title: Create Public Groups for Sharing Targets
Summary: Maintain reusable user populations that can be selected by supported sharing and access features.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Maintain reusable user populations that can be selected by supported sharing and access features.

Before you begin

Define the group's purpose and membership owner. Confirm whether direct users, roles, or other groups are the appropriate membership source for the business requirement.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Evaluate object permissions, field permissions, and record access as separate layers. Use a test user whose other grants are understood, including group membership and broad administrative access. A successful administrator test is insufficient evidence for a restricted business role.

Steps

  1. In Setup, find Public Groups and select New. Enter a descriptive label and group name that explain the population rather than the access level of one particular sharing rule.
  2. Add the required users, roles, or existing groups using the membership selectors. Review nested groups carefully so their indirect members do not expand the target unexpectedly.
  3. Review the available hierarchy-related option and choose it according to the approved sharing design. Do not assume group membership behaves exactly like a role assignment.
  4. Save the group and select it as the target in a separately reviewed sharing rule or another supported feature. Creating the group alone does not share every record with its members.
  5. Test with one direct member, one indirect member where nesting is used, and one nonmember. Check the actual records and access levels supplied by the consuming feature.
  6. Document who updates membership when staff move teams. Review group reuse before removing members, because several rules or folders can depend on the same group.

Example

A Regional Reviewers group can be referenced by multiple sharing rules. Adding a user to that group can affect every rule that targets it, even when the user was added for only one team request.

Verify the result

Confirm group membership matches the approved population and the dependent rule shares the intended records. Test a nonmember to ensure another access path is not masking a membership error.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If members cannot open records, check the actual sharing rule, recalculation, object permissions, and field access. If unexpected users receive access, inspect nested groups, roles, hierarchy behavior, and other independent shares.

Limitations

A public group is a membership container, not a profile or permission set. It does not by itself grant object permissions or make every record public.

Title: Design and Maintain a Role Hierarchy
Summary: Use roles to support the intended record-visibility hierarchy while keeping job permissions separate.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Use roles to support the intended record-visibility hierarchy while keeping job permissions separate.

Before you begin

Map who needs visibility into whose records and identify affected objects. Obtain a sharing-design review before changing a hierarchy used by many existing users.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Evaluate object permissions, field permissions, and record access as separate layers. Use a test user whose other grants are understood, including group membership and broad administrative access. A successful administrator test is insufficient evidence for a restricted business role.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Roles and review the current hierarchy. Start with record-visibility needs rather than reproducing every reporting line from the human-resources organization chart.
  2. Create or edit the role at the approved location and enter clear labels. Review supported object-specific access options presented by the role form.
  3. Assign the intended users and confirm each user's actual role. A profile controls permissions while a role participates in record access, so one cannot substitute for the other.
  4. Review organization-wide defaults and hierarchy behavior for the affected objects. For custom objects, inspect the relevant Grant Access Using Hierarchies setting rather than assuming all objects behave identically.
  5. Allow any sharing recalculation to complete and test owners, managers, and peer users with representative records. Include a negative case across a branch that should remain separate.
  6. Review sharing rules that target roles or roles and subordinates after restructuring. Document the change because moving one role can affect several downstream access paths.

Example

A regional manager can need visibility into representatives' opportunities without receiving the representatives' profile. Peer representatives may still have separate private records depending on the object's sharing model.

Verify the result

Confirm a manager receives intended record access, a peer user does not receive unintended access, and neither user gains unsupported object actions solely from a role assignment.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a manager cannot open a record, check object permissions, ownership, object-specific hierarchy behavior, and recalculation. If access is too broad, examine role-targeted sharing rules and View All or Modify All grants.

Limitations

Roles do not grant object or field permissions. Some objects inherit access from related records, so validate the actual object model instead of assuming ownership hierarchy explains every record.

Title: Create Queues for Shared Record Ownership
Summary: Let a team receive and work eligible records through a shared queue rather than one person's ownership.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Let a team receive and work eligible records through a shared queue rather than one person's ownership.

Before you begin

Choose a supported queue-enabled object and define the team that will take responsibility for queued records. Decide whether and how queue notifications should be sent.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Evaluate object permissions, field permissions, and record access as separate layers. Use a test user whose other grants are understood, including group membership and broad administrative access. A successful administrator test is insufficient evidence for a restricted business role.

Steps

  1. In Setup, search for Queues and select New. Enter a label and queue name that identify the workstream, such as inbound support or unqualified regional leads.
  2. Configure the queue email and member-notification options according to the team's operating process. Confirm the notification recipient is monitored and approved before sending test messages.
  3. Add the supported objects that the queue should own. Do not assume every standard or custom object can use queue ownership.
  4. Add the intended members using users, roles, or other available selectors. Review indirect membership and each member's object permissions before putting real work into the queue.
  5. Save and create a sample record owned by the queue, or use a separately configured assignment rule. Provide a suitable list view so users can find and accept the work.
  6. Test a member taking ownership and completing the task. Document triage responsibility so a queue does not become an unattended collection of records.

Example

An inbound case queue can hold new cases until an available support representative accepts ownership. The queue is the initial owner; membership and object permissions determine who can work the records.

Verify the result

Confirm the queue appears as an eligible owner for the selected object and a permitted member can find and accept a sample record. Check notification behavior with controlled recipients.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the queue cannot be selected, review supported objects and ownership restrictions. If a member cannot access a record, check object permissions, membership, applicable sharing behavior, and the record's current owner.

Limitations

Queues organize ownership for supported records. They do not automatically enable Omni-Channel routing or supply every permission a team member needs to edit the underlying object.

Title: Share an Individual Record Manually
Summary: Grant exceptional access to one supported record and verify the resulting access level.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Grant exceptional access to one supported record and verify the resulting access level.

Before you begin

Confirm the requester is authorized to share the record and the recipient has the necessary object permissions. Decide whether the requirement is a one-off exception or a repeatable sharing policy.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Evaluate object permissions, field permissions, and record access as separate layers. Use a test user whose other grants are understood, including group membership and broad administrative access. A successful administrator test is insufficient evidence for a restricted business role.

Steps

  1. Open the record in the intended app and find the supported sharing action or sharing controls. Availability depends on the object, page configuration, and your authority over the record.
  2. Select the intended user, role, or group and choose the least access level that supports the approved task. Review any related-record access options shown by the sharing dialog.
  3. Save the share and record the reason and review date through your team's exception process. Avoid using one-off sharing as a substitute for a common team-access rule.
  4. Ask the recipient to open the exact record and perform the intended read or edit task. Check field-level security separately if some values remain hidden or read-only.
  5. Inspect the sharing details where available to confirm the manual grant exists. Check whether ownership transfers or other lifecycle events can remove the manual share for this object.
  6. Remove the manual grant when the exception ends and retest access. If the recipient still has access, inspect other independent grants before concluding removal failed.

Example

A regional reviewer can receive read-only access to one account for an approved review without opening every regional account. A recurring need for all such accounts should prompt a sharing-design review.

Verify the result

Confirm the recipient can open only the intended record through this grant and cannot perform an excluded edit. After revocation, verify whether any independent access path legitimately remains.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the sharing action is unavailable, inspect object support, ownership, sharing model, and page actions. If access remains denied, review object permission and whether the recipient selected in the dialog is the intended user.

Limitations

Manual sharing opens access; it cannot restrict access already granted elsewhere. Some manual shares can be removed when ownership changes, so review lifecycle behavior before relying on long-term exceptions.

Title: Grant Account-Team Access to Collaborators
Summary: Use account teams to give named collaborators an explicit role and supported access on an account.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Use account teams to give named collaborators an explicit role and supported access on an account.

Before you begin

Confirm Account Teams is available and enabled for the org. Define team roles and approved access levels, and choose a sample account for testing.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Evaluate object permissions, field permissions, and record access as separate layers. Use a test user whose other grants are understood, including group membership and broad administrative access. A successful administrator test is insufficient evidence for a restricted business role.

Steps

  1. In Setup, find Account Teams and review the enablement settings and team-role values. Enable or adjust the feature only after the business owner has approved the collaboration model.
  2. Add the Account Team related list to the relevant account page layouts or supported page configuration. Confirm the intended users can see the team controls in their actual app.
  3. Open a test account and add a collaborator to its team. Select the appropriate team role and account access, plus supported opportunity or case access where the form offers those choices.
  4. Confirm the collaborator has object permissions needed for the intended work. Team membership supplies a record-access path rather than a complete collection of business permissions.
  5. Test the account and relevant related records with the collaborator. Use a peer account without a team grant to confirm the scope of the change.
  6. If default account teams are used, review how users apply them and maintain membership. Reassess existing account teams when collaborators change responsibilities rather than assuming defaults update all previous records.

Example

An account owner can add a technical specialist as a team member for one strategic customer. The specialist's team role describes the collaboration and should be paired with the approved access level.

Verify the result

Confirm the team entry names the correct user, role, and access levels. Test the specific account and related records, then compare another account outside the team's scope.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the related list is missing, review feature enablement and the assigned page layout. If the collaborator lacks access, inspect the team grant, object permissions, and the relevant related-record sharing behavior.

Limitations

Account teams and opportunity teams are separate features. A team role is descriptive and does not replace a user role, profile, permission set, or organization-wide sharing design.

Title: Diagnose Unexpected Record Access
Summary: Trace why a user can or cannot open a specific record before changing the sharing model.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Trace why a user can or cannot open a specific record before changing the sharing model.

Before you begin

Collect the exact user, record, required action, and actual result. Use a controlled test session and a reviewer authorized to inspect the user's effective permissions and sharing configuration.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Evaluate object permissions, field permissions, and record access as separate layers. Use a test user whose other grants are understood, including group membership and broad administrative access. A successful administrator test is insufficient evidence for a restricted business role.

Steps

  1. Check the user's license and object permissions first. Without the necessary Read or Edit permission, a sharing grant alone cannot authorize the task.
  2. Inspect field-level security if the record opens but a field is hidden or cannot be edited. Separate field access from record access before investigating the sharing model.
  3. Identify the record owner and organization-wide default for the object. Review whether access is inherited from a parent or is affected by the object's hierarchy behavior.
  4. Inspect roles, sharing rules, public groups, teams, queues, and manual shares that could reach the user. Use sharing details or access diagnostics where the object and org provide them.
  5. Check broad grants such as View All, Modify All, View All Data, and Modify All Data. These can explain access that a narrow sharing-rule review would otherwise miss.
  6. Change only the access source that conflicts with the requirement, then retest both an allowed and a denied record. Record the source responsible for the outcome so future troubleshooting starts from evidence.

Example

A user can retain access after removal from a sharing rule because they also own the record or hold a broad object permission. Adding another rule cannot explain or correct that excessive access.

Verify the result

Reproduce the original result and show which permission and record-access path enable the task. After a correction, verify intended access still works and the previously excessive access is removed.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If results differ between sessions, confirm the user, record, app, and completion of sharing recalculation. If only a custom page behaves differently, investigate its execution context and security enforcement with its owner.

Limitations

List filters, hidden navigation items, and page visibility rules are not record-security boundaries. Access can come from several independent sources, so removing one grant may not change the final result.

Title: Create a Custom Object for a New Business Record
Summary: Define a custom object only when an existing object cannot represent the business information appropriately.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Define a custom object only when an existing object cannot represent the business information appropriately.

Before you begin

Agree the record's purpose, owner, naming scheme, and expected relationships. Review standard objects first and obtain approval for the new data model.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review the object and field API names, existing data, and downstream consumers before a schema change. Reports, flows, imports, and integrations can depend on a field even when it is absent from the current page. Preserve stable identifiers wherever possible.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager and choose Create, then Custom Object. Enter a clear singular label, plural label, and object name that describe the business record.
  2. Choose the record-name field type, such as Text or Auto Number, based on how users should identify individual records. Add a description explaining the object's intended use.
  3. Review optional settings such as reports, activities, and field history according to the requirement. Select a deployment status appropriate for development rather than assuming immediate organization-wide availability.
  4. Save the object and add only the initial fields and relationships needed for the first use case. Review default record access in Sharing Settings before entering sensitive data.
  5. Create a tab when users need direct navigation and add it to the intended app. Grant object and field permissions through the appropriate access configuration; a tab does not grant those permissions.
  6. Create a sample record as a representative user, relate it to the required parent, and report on it if reporting is required. Document the object owner and naming conventions.

Example

A custom Equipment Request object can represent requests with their own lifecycle and owner. An additional Account field would be unsuitable if one account can have many independently managed requests.

Verify the result

Confirm users can create, read, and edit the intended record while an unauthorized user cannot. Check name generation, relationships, navigation, and report availability against the original requirement.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the object is absent from navigation, inspect tab visibility and app items. If it appears but cannot be opened or saved, inspect deployment status, object permissions, required fields, and validation rules.

Limitations

Creating an object adds schema, not an entire application. Security, automation, reporting, retention, and user navigation require separate decisions and validation.

Title: Create a Lookup Relationship Between Objects
Summary: Connect related records while preserving the ownership and lifecycle options of a lookup relationship.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Connect related records while preserving the ownership and lifecycle options of a lookup relationship.

Before you begin

Identify the child object that will store the reference and the target parent object. Decide whether the reference should be optional and what should happen if the referenced record is deleted.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review the object and field API names, existing data, and downstream consumers before a schema change. Reports, flows, imports, and integrations can depend on a field even when it is absent from the current page. Preserve stable identifiers wherever possible.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager, select the child object, and choose Fields & Relationships, then New. Choose Lookup Relationship and select the target object.
  2. Enter a descriptive label and review the generated API and child-relationship names. Choose names that make sense when the relationship is used in reports, automation, and integrations.
  3. Configure requiredness and supported deletion behavior deliberately. Read the options shown for the specific objects instead of assuming every lookup supports identical deletion rules.
  4. Configure any lookup filter needed to narrow eligible parent records. Decide whether an unmatched parent should block saving or simply guide selection, according to the available filter behavior.
  5. Set field-level security and page placement, then save. Add or review the related list on the parent layout if users need to browse child records from the parent.
  6. Create a child linked to a valid parent and test changing or clearing the link when allowed. Validate reporting and user access separately for the child and parent records.

Example

A request can look up an Account while retaining its own owner. The lookup identifies the customer but does not automatically make the request's sharing identical to the account's sharing.

Verify the result

Confirm the lookup stores the intended record reference, the parent related list displays the child when configured, and the agreed optional or required behavior is enforced.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a parent cannot be selected, check target-object permissions, record visibility, lookup filters, and record eligibility. If a related list is missing, inspect the parent layout rather than recreating the relationship.

Limitations

A lookup is not automatically a master-detail relationship. Do not assume cascade deletion, inherited sharing, or native roll-up summary eligibility without checking the actual relationship and object support.

Title: Create a Master-Detail Relationship Deliberately
Summary: Model a dependent child record when parent-controlled access and lifecycle behavior are appropriate.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Model a dependent child record when parent-controlled access and lifecycle behavior are appropriate.

Before you begin

Approve the deletion and ownership implications with the data owner. Confirm the object types support the relationship and inspect existing child records before selecting the creation or conversion route.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review the object and field API names, existing data, and downstream consumers before a schema change. Reports, flows, imports, and integrations can depend on a field even when it is absent from the current page. Preserve stable identifiers wherever possible.

Steps

  1. In Object Manager, select the proposed detail object and review existing records and relationships. Determine whether a direct new master-detail field is permitted or existing data first requires a populated lookup relationship.
  2. For a supported new relationship, create a Master-Detail Relationship field and select the master object. Read the limits and warnings presented for these particular objects.
  3. Set the label, relationship name, and sharing-related options offered by the wizard. Decide whether reparenting should be permitted rather than accepting it as an incidental default.
  4. Review how detail access and ownership are controlled by the master. Confirm that this matches the business requirement before saving and exposing the relationship.
  5. Add the field and related list to the relevant pages and test a parent with multiple detail records. If summarization is required, review native roll-up summary support on the master.
  6. In a test org, test attempted creation without a parent, access through different users, and the impact of deleting a sample parent. Use disposable data for lifecycle testing.

Example

A request line that has no useful existence without its request can be a detail record. A customer interaction that must survive independently may need a different relationship design.

Verify the result

Confirm every detail has a valid master, access follows the approved model, and parent lifecycle behavior matches the design. Verify reparenting behavior with a disposable record if it was enabled.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If relationship creation or conversion is blocked, inspect existing data, unsupported objects, existing master-detail fields, and dependent roll-ups. Do not delete business records simply to get past a schema error.

Limitations

Master-detail can cause detail records to be deleted with their master and changes ownership behavior. Relationship conversions have restrictions and require a separate impact review for populated objects.

Title: Create a Formula Field for a Calculated Value
Summary: Display a calculation derived from record data without asking users to maintain a duplicate value.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Display a calculation derived from record data without asking users to maintain a duplicate value.

Before you begin

Define the exact calculation, output type, blank-value behavior, and intended audience. Identify every referenced field and review whether the result could expose sensitive information.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review the object and field API names, existing data, and downstream consumers before a schema change. Reports, flows, imports, and integrations can depend on a field even when it is absent from the current page. Preserve stable identifiers wherever possible.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager, select the object, and create a new Formula field through Fields & Relationships. Enter a label and choose the return type that matches the result.
  2. Build the expression with Insert Field and the available functions. Use API field references from the editor and check data types instead of manually guessing names or converting every input to text.
  3. Decide how blanks should behave and use explicit handling when necessary. For a numeric calculation, test zero and missing values separately before treating them as equivalent business situations.
  4. Use Check Syntax and inspect any errors or limits reported by the formula editor. Keep the calculation understandable and add help text describing the business meaning rather than only the expression.
  5. Configure field-level security and page placement. Review access to the calculated result independently, especially when it references sensitive fields or related records.
  6. Save and test with normal, blank, zero, and boundary inputs. Change a source value and confirm the displayed result responds as expected without a separate data-entry task.

Example

On a custom request, a formula can calculate an estimated total from quantity and unit estimate. The design must specify what a blank quantity means before choosing whether the result should be blank or zero.

Verify the result

Compare several calculated results with a hand-worked expected answer. Check formatting, decimal precision, blank handling, and visibility for users with different permissions.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If syntax fails, check return types and field references. If the result is unexpected, inspect blank handling, formula evaluation rules, and source data before adding automation to overwrite what should remain a calculated field.

Limitations

Formula fields are read-only calculated values rather than manually editable stored inputs. Date-sensitive formulas can change as time changes, so use a stored snapshot when the business requires a historical value.

Title: Summarize Child Records with a Roll-Up Summary Field
Summary: Count or aggregate eligible detail records on their master using a native roll-up summary.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Count or aggregate eligible detail records on their master using a native roll-up summary.

Before you begin

Identify a supported master-detail relationship and the required aggregation. Confirm the child field type supports the chosen operation and define which detail records should be included.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review the object and field API names, existing data, and downstream consumers before a schema change. Reports, flows, imports, and integrations can depend on a field even when it is absent from the current page. Preserve stable identifiers wherever possible.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager and select the master object. In Fields & Relationships, create a Roll-Up Summary field if the relationship and object support that field type.
  2. Choose the related detail object and the required operation, such as COUNT, SUM, MIN, or MAX. Select an eligible detail field when the operation needs one.
  3. Configure filter criteria when only certain detail records should contribute. Translate the business rule into explicit conditions, including treatment of blank values and inactive or canceled items.
  4. Enter a descriptive label, help text, and field access. Put the result on the relevant page and consider reports or validation rules that will depend on the total.
  5. Save and create a small controlled set of detail records. Include matching and nonmatching records with values whose expected total can be calculated by hand.
  6. Edit, add, and delete disposable detail records to test recalculation. Review downstream automation on the master because an updated summary can affect other business behavior.

Example

A request can show the sum of approved request-line estimates while excluding canceled lines. Testing one approved line and one canceled line reveals whether the filter reflects the intended rule.

Verify the result

Compare the summary against the exact detail records included by the filter. Confirm recalculation after a qualifying child change and verify users can see the summary only where appropriate.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the detail object is unavailable, inspect the actual relationship type and object support. If the total is wrong, check the filter, selected aggregation field, qualifying records, and any recalculation still in progress.

Limitations

Native roll-up summaries generally require supported master-detail relationships or supported standard relationships. Do not assume an arbitrary lookup can be summarized through this field wizard.

Title: Configure Dependent Picklists
Summary: Limit a dependent field's selectable values according to a controlling field.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Limit a dependent field's selectable values according to a controlling field.

Before you begin

Define the controlling values and allowed dependent choices as a matrix. Confirm the fields and data types support dependencies and review existing records for combinations that no longer fit.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review the object and field API names, existing data, and downstream consumers before a schema change. Reports, flows, imports, and integrations can depend on a field even when it is absent from the current page. Preserve stable identifiers wherever possible.

Steps

  1. In Object Manager, select the object and inspect both fields in Fields & Relationships. Confirm the controlling field and dependent picklist are suitable for a dependency.
  2. Open Field Dependencies and select New. Choose the controlling field and dependent field, then continue to the dependency matrix.
  3. Include the permitted dependent values for each controlling value and exclude combinations the business does not want users to choose. Review blank or default behavior explicitly.
  4. Use Preview where available to test each controlling value before saving. A small approved matrix is easier to validate than a large configuration built by trial and error.
  5. Review record-type picklist availability for both fields. A dependency cannot offer a dependent value that is unavailable for the current record type.
  6. Save and test create and edit forms as a representative user. Review import and integration behavior separately and clean existing invalid combinations through an approved data-quality process.

Example

A Request Category of Hardware can offer Laptop and Monitor, while Software offers License and Access. The record type must also permit those choices or the dependency alone will not display them.

Verify the result

Test every controlling value, an empty controlling value where allowed, and each relevant record type. Confirm the dependent choices match the approved matrix in the actual editing surface.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a value is missing, inspect whether it is active, enabled for the record type, and included in the dependency matrix. If invalid combinations already exist, investigate their creation path instead of assuming saving a dependency repairs historical data.

Limitations

Dependencies guide supported picklist selection surfaces. They do not replace a validation rule when a business combination must be enforced across all data-entry and integration paths.

Title: Reuse Picklist Choices with a Global Value Set
Summary: Maintain a shared vocabulary for custom picklist fields without creating a separate reference-data object.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Maintain a shared vocabulary for custom picklist fields without creating a separate reference-data object.

Before you begin

Agree a vocabulary owner and identify the fields that truly share the same meaning. Review integrations that depend on picklist API values before consolidating existing choices.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review the object and field API names, existing data, and downstream consumers before a schema change. Reports, flows, imports, and integrations can depend on a field even when it is absent from the current page. Preserve stable identifiers wherever possible.

Steps

  1. In Setup, find Picklist Value Sets and select New. Enter a clear label, name, and description explaining the common business meaning of the values.
  2. Add the approved values and review their labels, API names, ordering, and default choice. Keep stable identifiers where integrations already rely on them.
  3. In Object Manager, create a supported custom Picklist field and choose the option to use a global picklist value set. Select the approved set instead of defining a second independent list.
  4. Configure field access and page placement, then review the choices available to each record type. Sharing a global set does not automatically make every choice available in every record type.
  5. Test at least two fields that use the set and confirm a deliberate vocabulary update appears where expected. Include any dependent-picklist rules that reference the affected fields.
  6. Document the set's consumers and change owner. Review the impact on existing records and integrations before deactivating, replacing, or renaming values.

Example

Several custom objects can use the same approved Priority vocabulary. A change to that global set can affect all of those fields, which is useful only when the meanings should remain aligned.

Verify the result

Confirm each intended field references the same global set and record-type choices remain correct. Test a saved record and an integration sample using the expected API value.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a field offers unexpected choices, inspect its value-set source, active values, record-type restrictions, and dependencies. Review conversion restrictions before trying to move an existing independent picklist into a shared set.

Limitations

A global value set is a shared vocabulary rather than a lookup table with additional attributes. Converting existing fields and deleting shared values have restrictions and need impact analysis.

Title: Track Changes to Important Fields
Summary: Enable field history for supported fields and show future tracked changes to authorized users.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Enable field history for supported fields and show future tracked changes to authorized users.

Before you begin

Choose the object and a small set of fields whose change history matters. Review field-type eligibility, available tracking limits, and retention needs before treating history as an audit solution.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review the object and field API names, existing data, and downstream consumers before a schema change. Reports, flows, imports, and integrations can depend on a field even when it is absent from the current page. Preserve stable identifiers wherever possible.

Steps

  1. In Object Manager, select the object and open Fields & Relationships. Use Set History Tracking or the equivalent supported control for that object.
  2. Enable history tracking where required and select the eligible fields. Prioritize changes with a business reason, such as owner-facing status or a key reference, instead of selecting fields without an audit use case.
  3. Save and add the object's History related list to the appropriate page layout or supported record page. Confirm the intended users can see both the record and the relevant history surface.
  4. Edit a tracked field on a test record and save. Change it again with a different authorized user when that helps verify attribution and timing.
  5. Inspect the history entry for the changed field, actor, timestamp, and supported old and new values. Compare display time zones before interpreting the sequence of events.
  6. Document when tracking was enabled and how long the organization needs to retain changes. Assess separately whether licensed extended-audit capabilities or exports are required.

Example

Tracking a request's Status can show who moved it from New to Approved after tracking began. It will not reconstruct status changes that occurred before the field was selected for tracking.

Verify the result

Confirm a new supported change creates a history entry and untracked fields do not appear unexpectedly. Check the History related list as a representative reader rather than only as an administrator.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If nothing appears, verify tracking was enabled before the test, the field is selected, and the value actually changed. Some field types record limited details; inspect the documented behavior before assuming data was lost.

Limitations

Field history is prospective and has field-type, quantity, and retention limits. It is distinct from Setup Audit Trail, which tracks supported administrative configuration changes.

Title: Choose the Right Way to Require a Field
Summary: Select field-level, page-level, or conditional validation according to where the requirement must apply.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Select field-level, page-level, or conditional validation according to where the requirement must apply.

Before you begin

Define when the value is mandatory and which write paths must enforce it. Inventory existing blanks, imports, integrations, flows, record types, and page configurations before adding a requirement.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review the object and field API names, existing data, and downstream consumers before a schema change. Reports, flows, imports, and integrations can depend on a field even when it is absent from the current page. Preserve stable identifiers wherever possible.

Steps

  1. In Object Manager, inspect the field's type and supported requiredness options. Determine whether the value should always be present on every record or only under specific business conditions.
  2. For a universally required custom field where supported, evaluate field-level requiredness. Review the consequences for existing records and every creation or update path before enabling it.
  3. For a requirement limited to a supported UI experience, review the page-layout or Dynamic Forms field requirement. Check every assigned page and do not treat UI-only requiredness as an API constraint.
  4. For a conditional business requirement, design a validation rule whose error condition is true when the required value is missing. Use an actionable message and test transitions into and out of the condition.
  5. Prepare a backfill or migration plan for existing records where necessary. Coordinate changes with integration owners rather than discovering missing values through production failures.
  6. Test the UI, a representative import or API write, and relevant automation. Include valid, missing, and condition-not-applicable scenarios before activation.

Example

A cancellation reason may be required only when Status is Canceled. A conditional validation rule can express that business requirement more accurately than making the field mandatory on every record.

Verify the result

Confirm the selected mechanism blocks the intended invalid writes and permits legitimate scenarios. Verify the error message directs users to the missing field and check existing records can still be maintained.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If only one page blocks the save, inspect page-level settings. If imports fail unexpectedly, inspect field requiredness, validation rules, and automation-generated values instead of assuming page layout requirements apply to all writes.

Limitations

Requiredness can interact with field permissions and hidden UI sections. Avoid making a value mandatory for users who have no supported way to provide or derive it.

Title: Create a Lightning App for a Team
Summary: Give a team a focused application with approved navigation and branding.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Give a team a focused application with approved navigation and branding.

Before you begin

List the objects and pages the team uses most and identify the target user population. Decide whether standard navigation or a supported console experience fits the work.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Test in the actual Lightning app with the intended profile and record type. Builder previews do not reproduce every permission or assignment. Keep security decisions in permissions and sharing, and use page configuration to make authorized work easier to find.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open App Manager and choose New Lightning App. Enter a clear name and description that distinguish this app from similar workspaces.
  2. Configure the available branding options using approved assets. Choose navigation and supported application options according to the team's workflow rather than adding every feature by default.
  3. Select the navigation items users need, such as Accounts, Cases, Reports, or a custom tab. Put frequent tasks near the beginning and remove items that belong to another team.
  4. Review profile availability in the app wizard and any applicable application visibility grants. App visibility and underlying object access must both be configured for the intended users.
  5. Save and launch the application from App Launcher as a representative user. Confirm the expected navigation items are present and the relevant objects and pages actually open.
  6. Review assigned Home and record pages where the app needs a different experience. Document the app owner and navigation purpose so later requests do not turn the app into an unstructured list.

Example

A service workspace can prioritize Cases, Accounts, Knowledge, and Reports. Its navigation helps users find work, while permission sets and record sharing determine what data they can access.

Verify the result

Confirm a permitted user can find and open the app, complete the main workflow, and navigate between the selected items. Check a user outside the intended audience against the approved visibility design.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the app is missing, inspect application visibility, profile availability, and license support. If an item opens with an access error, inspect object and record permissions rather than adding more navigation entries.

Limitations

An application is a workspace, not a security boundary. Hiding an app or tab does not revoke data access through another app, a report, or an authorized API client.

Title: Add a Custom Object Tab to Navigation
Summary: Make an existing custom object discoverable in the intended Lightning app.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Make an existing custom object discoverable in the intended Lightning app.

Before you begin

Have an existing custom object, an approved audience, and object permissions ready for testing. Confirm the requirement is navigation rather than a new data model.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Test in the actual Lightning app with the intended profile and record type. Builder previews do not reproduce every permission or assignment. Keep security decisions in permissions and sharing, and use page configuration to make authorized work easier to find.

Steps

  1. In Setup, search for Tabs and locate Custom Object Tabs. Create a tab for the intended custom object if one does not already exist.
  2. Choose an appropriate tab style and complete the wizard. Review profile tab visibility and the application selections shown rather than exposing the tab everywhere by default.
  3. Open App Manager, edit the target Lightning app, and add the tab to its navigation items. Place it where it fits the team's workflow and save.
  4. Review the intended users' tab settings and object permissions. A visible navigation item is useful only when those users can perform the supported object tasks.
  5. Open the app as a representative user and check both its navigation menu and App Launcher. Review user personalization if a user-specific navigation arrangement obscures the change.
  6. Create or open a sample record from the new tab and confirm the correct record page appears. Tell users which app contains the object so they do not rely on a memorized direct link.

Example

After creating an Equipment Request object, a tab can make its list view available in the Operations app. Creating the object alone does not guarantee that users will find it in their app navigation.

Verify the result

Confirm the tab appears in the correct app and opens the object list without errors. Test creation or reading as the intended audience and check that unrelated users follow the approved access model.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the tab is absent, inspect whether it exists, its visibility setting, app navigation, and user personalization. If access is denied after selecting it, inspect object permissions, deployment status, and applicable record sharing.

Limitations

A tab is an entry point rather than a permission grant. Users can have object access without a tab, and hiding the tab does not secure the underlying records.

Title: Customize a Lightning Home Page
Summary: Provide a useful landing page and activate it for the intended app and user population.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Provide a useful landing page and activate it for the intended app and user population.

Before you begin

Agree the audience and the small set of information or tasks the page should prioritize. Identify existing Home page assignments and any components that require additional licenses or permissions.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Test in the actual Lightning app with the intended profile and record type. Builder previews do not reproduce every permission or assignment. Keep security decisions in permissions and sharing, and use page configuration to make authorized work easier to find.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Lightning App Builder and create a Home Page, or clone an appropriate existing Home page. Choose a template suited to the information density and expected devices.
  2. Add supported standard components that serve the agreed tasks. Prefer a few relevant components over placing every available chart, list, and assistant on the initial screen.
  3. Configure each component and check the data it displays. Review dashboard visibility and execution behavior separately when embedding analytics.
  4. Save with a descriptive name and use Activate to select the intended org, app, or app-and-profile assignment options offered by the activation wizard.
  5. Open the actual app as a target user and select Home. Check loading, useful content, and behavior at the expected screen sizes rather than relying only on the builder preview.
  6. Compare existing assignments before rollout and document how to restore the previous page assignment. Ask a representative user to complete the key task from the new landing page.

Example

A support Home page can surface the team's recent cases and approved operating guidance. A sales Home page can have a different focus without replacing the Home page for every user in the org.

Verify the result

Confirm the new page appears for the intended app and profile combination and another combination still gets its expected page. Verify embedded content is useful and accessible to the actual audience.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If users see the previous page, inspect activation and assignment precedence and confirm the app they opened. If a component is blank, inspect its configuration, feature entitlement, data permissions, and supported device behavior.

Limitations

Saving a page and activating it are separate steps. A Home page arranges information; it does not grant access to the reports, records, or licensed features displayed inside it.

Title: Choose Fields for a Standard Highlights Panel
Summary: Use a compact layout to control key fields shown by supported standard record highlights.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Use a compact layout to control key fields shown by supported standard record highlights.

Before you begin

Identify the object, supported highlights component, and highest-priority fields. Check whether the page uses the standard Highlights Panel or a Dynamic Highlights Panel before choosing the configuration tool.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Test in the actual Lightning app with the intended profile and record type. Builder previews do not reproduce every permission or assignment. Keep security decisions in permissions and sharing, and use page configuration to make authorized work easier to find.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager, select the object, and open Compact Layouts. Review the current primary compact layout and any record-type assignments.
  2. Create or clone a compact layout with a descriptive name. Select the most useful eligible fields and put the key identifier first, followed by information users need at a glance.
  3. Save and open Compact Layout Assignment. Set the primary layout and supported record-type overrides according to the requirement.
  4. Review the actual Lightning record page in App Builder. Confirm it uses a standard component that reads compact-layout information rather than a different highlights implementation.
  5. Open records with different record types as a representative user. Check which fields fit at the available width and whether field-level security hides any selected values.
  6. Test the supported mobile experience if mobile users depend on the same compact layout. Adjust field priority rather than assuming every selected field appears on every screen.

Example

For a request, the standard highlights panel might emphasize Name, Status, Priority, and Owner. The wider page layout can still contain many more fields below those key values.

Verify the result

Confirm the intended layout assignment is active and the most important permitted values appear in the standard highlights panel. Compare at least two record types when overrides are configured.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the display does not change, inspect the page's highlights component and compact-layout assignment. For a Dynamic Highlights Panel, inspect its fields in Lightning App Builder instead of repeatedly editing the compact layout.

Limitations

Compact layouts do not define the full Details form or replace field-level security. Displayed field counts and behavior vary by component, form factor, and supported object.

Title: Create an Object-Specific Quick Action
Summary: Give users a focused action for creating or updating a record in its current context.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Give users a focused action for creating or updating a record in its current context.

Before you begin

Define the task, target object, required fields, and intended launch record. Confirm the action type is supported for the object and expected interface.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Test in the actual Lightning app with the intended profile and record type. Builder previews do not reproduce every permission or assignment. Keep security decisions in permissions and sharing, and use page configuration to make authorized work easier to find.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager for the source object and select Buttons, Links, and Actions. Choose New Action and select the appropriate supported action type.
  2. For a create action, select the target object and relationship context offered by the form. For an update action, choose the source object's supported update action and enter a clear label.
  3. Edit the action layout so it includes fields users need to complete the task. Keep required inputs visible and check field-level security for the intended audience.
  4. Configure predefined field values only when they match an approved business rule. Consider whether a user should be able to override the value and whether automation will change it after save.
  5. Add the action to the assigned page layout's Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience Actions section, or configure it through Dynamic Actions when the page uses that mechanism.
  6. Test from the actual source record as a representative user. Confirm the related record is linked correctly, defaults are sensible, and validation errors can be resolved within the action.

Example

An account-specific New Request action can create a request already related to the account. Users still need permission to create the request and access its required fields.

Verify the result

Confirm the action appears in the intended location, opens the expected fields, and saves a correctly related record. Check a missing required value and a valid submission.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the action is absent, inspect page-layout assignment, Dynamic Actions, action type support, and target-object permissions. If saving fails, inspect validation rules, required fields, predefined values, and automation.

Limitations

An action layout differs from the object's full page layout. A displayed action does not bypass object permissions, field access, record access, or record validation.

Title: Create a Global Quick Action
Summary: Offer a supported creation task without requiring users to open a source record first.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Offer a supported creation task without requiring users to open a source record first.

Before you begin

Choose a task that does not require an implicit parent-record context. Identify the target object and all fields the user must provide without that context.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Test in the actual Lightning app with the intended profile and record type. Builder previews do not reproduce every permission or assignment. Keep security decisions in permissions and sharing, and use page configuration to make authorized work easier to find.

Steps

  1. In Setup, find Global Actions and select New Action. Choose a supported global action type and the target object, then enter a clear label and name.
  2. Review the record-type choice when the action requires one. Ensure the intended users can use that record type and provide every required value.
  3. Configure the action layout with the essential fields and supported defaults. If the new record needs a parent relationship, include a field the user can explicitly populate.
  4. Add the action to the appropriate global publisher layout through Publisher Layouts. Review layout assignments and where the global action is supported in the intended interface.
  5. Open the global action menu as a representative user and run the task. Confirm a record is created with the expected owner, record type, and explicitly supplied relationships.
  6. Review the result in the target object's list view and record page. Update the action if the user must leave it to fix routine required information.

Example

A global New Request action can let a user enter a request from any supported page. Unlike an account-specific action, it should not be expected to infer which account the user meant.

Verify the result

Confirm the action appears for the intended user, requires the appropriate inputs, and saves a valid record. Inspect any parent lookup to ensure the relationship came from an explicit value or designed default.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the action is missing, inspect publisher layout assignment, object permissions, record-type availability, and surface support. If the wrong default appears, inspect the action's predefined values and subsequent automation.

Limitations

Global actions do not automatically inherit the currently viewed record as their source context. Use an object-specific action when the relationship to the launch record is an essential part of the task.

Title: Use Dynamic Forms on a Supported Record Page
Summary: Arrange individual fields and sections in Lightning App Builder for a focused record experience.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Arrange individual fields and sections in Lightning App Builder for a focused record experience.

Before you begin

Confirm the object supports Dynamic Forms by checking the Fields tab in Lightning App Builder. Inventory required fields and the existing page-layout behavior before migrating a production page.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Test in the actual Lightning app with the intended profile and record type. Builder previews do not reproduce every permission or assignment. Keep security decisions in permissions and sharing, and use page configuration to make authorized work easier to find.

Steps

  1. Open a record page in Lightning App Builder and clone the page for a controlled trial. Review its current Record Detail component and activation assignments.
  2. Where available, use Upgrade Now on Record Detail to migrate fields from a chosen page layout, or build field sections directly from the Fields tab.
  3. Arrange field sections around user tasks and remove duplicate presentations. Keep fields that are always required available through a supported input path.
  4. Configure visibility rules only where they improve usability and test changes in controlling values. Document that field visibility rules organize the interface rather than securing the data.
  5. Review actions, related lists, and other page-layout-dependent behavior separately. Migrating record fields does not move every page-layout responsibility into Dynamic Forms.
  6. Save, activate for a limited audience, and test creation, editing, and supported mobile behavior. Compare a permitted reader with an editor and check fields that are conditionally hidden.

Example

An opportunity page can separate essential fields from secondary information and display a specialized section only for a relevant record condition. The underlying field permissions still control who may retrieve those values.

Verify the result

Confirm users can complete the full record lifecycle without an inaccessible required field. Check the active app and profile assignment, visibility transitions, and the supported form factors.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the Fields tab is absent, check object support before attempting migration. If a save fails, inspect missing required values, field permissions, validation rules, and hidden sections rather than simply restoring every field.

Limitations

Dynamic Forms is not supported uniformly across every object or surface. Keep a tested rollback page assignment and verify current supported behavior in the target org before replacing an established page.

Title: Show Components with Visibility Rules
Summary: Display relevant Lightning record-page components according to supported conditions.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Display relevant Lightning record-page components according to supported conditions.

Before you begin

Define the condition and identify the information needed to evaluate it. Confirm that hiding the component is a usability requirement rather than the only proposed protection for sensitive data.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Test in the actual Lightning app with the intended profile and record type. Builder previews do not reproduce every permission or assignment. Keep security decisions in permissions and sharing, and use page configuration to make authorized work easier to find.

Steps

  1. Open the relevant record page in Lightning App Builder and select the component to control. Review the component's existing settings and any current visibility filters.
  2. Add supported visibility filters using the properties pane. Choose record, user, permission, or device conditions offered for that component and page type.
  3. Set the filter combination deliberately. When using multiple filters, confirm whether all conditions, any condition, or custom logic should determine visibility.
  4. Preview the layout and test the rule with records and users on both sides of the condition. Include empty values and a change from a matching value to a nonmatching value.
  5. Check any condition that depends on a field the user cannot access. Verify observed behavior instead of assuming an inaccessible field evaluates the same way for every audience.
  6. Save and activate the intended assignment, then test the actual runtime page. Confirm that hiding the component leaves the remaining page understandable and does not conceal an essential task.

Example

A specialist guidance component can appear when a request is marked Complex. Users viewing ordinary requests should still have a clear page without a blank area or unexplained missing controls.

Verify the result

Test a matching record, a nonmatching record, and a user with different permissions. Check the page after relevant data changes and confirm the intended assignment is active.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the component never appears, inspect filter values, custom logic, field access, and the actual page assignment. If it appears unexpectedly, check whether another component instance exists without the same visibility rule.

Limitations

Visibility rules do not revoke access to underlying records or fields. Users may still reach the information through reports, other pages, or authorized APIs unless the security model restricts it.

Title: Create and Share a Useful List View
Summary: Build a focused object list with meaningful filters, columns, and audience settings.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Build a focused object list with meaningful filters, columns, and audience settings.

Before you begin

Define the work queue or question the list should support. Identify a supported object and confirm the creator has permission to create and, if needed, share list views.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.
