Test in the actual Lightning app with the intended profile and record type. Builder previews do not reproduce every permission or assignment. Keep security decisions in permissions and sharing, and use page configuration to make authorized work easier to find.

Steps

  1. Open the object's tab in Lightning Experience and use List View Controls to create a new view or clone a suitable existing view. Give it a descriptive name tied to the work.
  2. Choose who can see the list view using the available private, public, or group sharing controls. Review whether your permissions allow a shared view before designing it for a whole team.
  3. Set record-scope filters such as ownership and add explicit field filters. Use filter logic where needed and test blank values instead of assuming every active record matches the intended criteria.
  4. Select useful columns and sort order. Include the fields needed to decide the next action, while respecting field permissions and supported list-view capabilities.
  5. Save and test with the intended users. Confirm that a shared definition returns each user's permitted records rather than assuming everyone sees the creator's rows.
  6. Pin the view if appropriate for personal navigation and document its purpose. Review it when business statuses change so old filters do not quietly hide new work.

Example

An Open High-Priority Requests view can filter for unfinished requests and a high-priority value. The same shared list definition can return different rows for users with different record access.

Verify the result

Check a record that should match and one that should not. Test another user's view, inspect the visible columns, and confirm users can open the returned records.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If expected rows are missing, inspect ownership scope, filter logic, field values, and sharing. If inline edit is unavailable, inspect supported fields, record types, permissions, and view conditions rather than assuming the list is broken.

Limitations

List-view sharing shares the definition rather than the underlying records. List filters and tab visibility cannot be used to enforce record security.

Title: Prepare a CSV File for Salesforce Import
Summary: Clean source data and map it to verified Salesforce fields before starting a data load.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Clean source data and map it to verified Salesforce fields before starting a data load.

Before you begin

Identify the target object, import tool, operation, and data owner. Export a backup for updates and choose a small representative pilot containing typical and exceptional rows.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Preserve the source file and record identifiers, and keep per-row results for any write operation. Start with a reviewed pilot, reconcile partial success, and identify a recovery owner. A completed data job can still contain rejected rows or incorrect business mappings.

Steps

  1. Review the target object's actual fields, required values, active picklist choices, and relationships. Decide whether each source column maps to an existing field or should be excluded.
  2. Use a CSV format supported by the chosen tool and preserve the required encoding. Keep identifiers, leading zeros, and long record IDs as text so spreadsheet software does not silently alter them.
  3. Normalize dates, date-times, numbers, and picklist API values to the tool's documented input format. Make the source time zone explicit for date-time values.
  4. Remove unintended blank rows and duplicate records, then validate required fields. Decide how blank input should affect existing values; different operations and tool settings can handle blanks differently.
  5. Resolve parent relationships using the correct Salesforce IDs or supported external-ID matching. Do not treat a parent's display name as a reliable unique key without a deliberate matching design.
  6. Save a pilot file and mapping, run it in a test environment, and reconcile each row with the result. Keep the original source file unchanged for traceability.

Example

An account number such as 001234 must remain text throughout preparation. If a spreadsheet converts it to 1234, the import can create the wrong match even when the CSV is otherwise valid.

Verify the result

Check row count, identifiers, required values, representative dates, and parent matches before loading. Compare pilot results with the intended create or update operation and examine every rejected row.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If columns shift, inspect delimiters and quoted commas or line breaks. If values are rejected, compare the actual field API names, picklist values, formats, and validation rules rather than renaming columns at random.

Limitations

Preparing a CSV does not disable validation or automation. Use the chosen tool's current format requirements and protect exports according to their data classification.

Title: Import Supported Records with Data Import Wizard
Summary: Load a modest set of supported records through the guided import interface.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Load a modest set of supported records through the guided import interface.

Before you begin

Prepare a clean CSV and confirm the object and operation are supported by Data Import Wizard. Verify the user's import permissions and check the wizard's current record limit.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Preserve the source file and record identifiers, and keep per-row results for any write operation. Start with a reviewed pilot, reconcile partial success, and identify a recovery owner. A completed data job can still contain rejected rows or incorrect business mappings.

Steps

  1. In Setup, find Data Import Wizard and launch the wizard. Select the appropriate standard or custom object from the available choices rather than assuming every object can be imported here.
  2. Choose whether to add new records, update existing records, or use a supported combined mode. Read the matching options because they determine whether source rows create duplicates or update existing records.
  3. Upload the prepared pilot CSV and select the matching and ownership options required by the task. Confirm the environment and target object before continuing.
  4. Review every field mapping, especially required fields, record identifiers, parent references, and picklists. Explicitly ignore columns that must not be loaded.
  5. Review the summary and start the pilot import. Follow the job status and download or inspect the available result information to identify successes and failures.
  6. Open representative records and reconcile the pilot before processing the full approved file. Retain the mapping, source file, and results so any correction targets only the affected rows.

Example

A small contact import can match existing records through the wizard's supported matching options. A successful upload does not by itself prove that each contact was linked to the correct account.

Verify the result

Confirm input rows reconcile with successful and failed outcomes. Inspect new and updated records, parent relationships, ownership, and duplicate behavior before repeating the operation on more data.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the object or operation is unavailable, choose another supported tool rather than altering the file to imitate a different object. If rows fail, inspect required fields, mapping, validation rules, and the detailed results.

Limitations

The wizard supports a defined set of objects and operations and has volume limits. It is not a universal importer, and completing a job does not guarantee every input row succeeded.

Title: Insert and Update Records with Data Loader
Summary: Use an approved API-based tool for controlled record creation or updates with saved mappings and results.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Use an approved API-based tool for controlled record creation or updates with saved mappings and results.

Before you begin

Use an approved Data Loader installation and a user with API and object access. Prepare a backup for updates, a clean CSV, and a pilot sized to review row by row.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Preserve the source file and record identifiers, and keep per-row results for any write operation. Start with a reviewed pilot, reconcile partial success, and identify a recovery owner. A completed data job can still contain rejected rows or incorrect business mappings.

Steps

  1. Open Data Loader and choose Insert only for new records or Update for records identified by Salesforce IDs. Do not use Insert merely because an existing-record matching strategy has not been defined.
  2. Authenticate to the intended environment through the approved login method. Verify the org identity before continuing to object and file selection.
  3. Select the target object and pilot CSV, then map fields deliberately. For Update, map the record Id and include only fields the task is authorized to change.
  4. Review settings that affect batch handling, blank values, and operation mode. Consult the installed tool's behavior rather than assuming defaults match another import tool.
  5. Select an approved location for success and error files, execute the pilot, and inspect the per-row results. Record created IDs and failed-row reasons before considering a retry.
  6. Verify sample records and reconcile counts, then process the remaining approved rows. Retry only corrected failures when the initial operation partly succeeded.

Example

An update file containing account IDs and a single approved classification field should update those accounts without reloading unrelated columns from an old export. Minimal update payloads reduce accidental overwrites.

Verify the result

Confirm each successful result maps to the intended record and field changes. Compare total input rows with successes and failures, then test ownership, relationships, and automation-sensitive fields.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If login fails, inspect API entitlement, authentication route, and network policy. If rows fail, read the error CSV for permission, required-field, validation, or relationship errors before repeating the job.

Limitations

API data loads can trigger business automation and create partial success. Keep success files and backups; a second full Insert job can duplicate rows that already succeeded.

Title: Use an External ID for Repeatable Upserts
Summary: Match source-system records through a stable identifier so repeat loads can update rather than duplicate them.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Match source-system records through a stable identifier so repeat loads can update rather than duplicate them.

Before you begin

Choose a stable source key and a supported field marked External ID. Decide whether uniqueness must be enforced and review duplicate key values before the first load.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Preserve the source file and record identifiers, and keep per-row results for any write operation. Start with a reviewed pilot, reconcile partial success, and identify a recovery owner. A completed data job can still contain rejected rows or incorrect business mappings.

Steps

  1. In Object Manager, inspect the candidate external-ID field and its data type. Confirm that stored source values are stable identifiers rather than names that users routinely change.
  2. Review existing Salesforce records and the source file for duplicate keys. Where the business requires one record per source key, assess a Unique constraint separately from the External ID attribute.
  3. Prepare the pilot CSV with the external-ID column and only the fields to create or update. Preserve leading zeros and case according to the field's configured matching behavior.
  4. In a supported tool such as Data Loader, choose Upsert and select the intended external-ID field as the matching field. Review relationship mappings independently.
  5. Run the pilot and record whether each row was inserted or updated. Repeat the same pilot and confirm existing records are matched rather than created again.
  6. Retain the source-key mapping and successful Salesforce IDs. Define how missing keys and source-system key changes will be handled before scheduling repeat loads.

Example

A customer reference such as ERP-004281 can identify the same account on successive exports. Changing that key without a migration design can make a later upsert treat the customer as a new record.

Verify the result

Verify one new-key row inserts and one existing-key row updates the intended record. Repeat the file and check that the count remains stable and no source key has matched multiple records.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If matching is ambiguous, inspect duplicate key values and the chosen external-ID field. If duplicates appear, confirm the tool used Upsert and the intended matching field rather than Insert or another identifier.

Limitations

External ID and Unique are separate field properties. Upsert does not automatically reconcile conflicting business records or remove duplicates already present in the organization.

Title: Configure Matching Rules and Duplicate Rules
Summary: Define how potential duplicates are recognized and what should happen when a user saves one.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Define how potential duplicates are recognized and what should happen when a user saves one.

Before you begin

Choose a supported object and a clear definition of a duplicate. Identify legitimate similar records, data-entry paths, and the impact of blocking creates or updates.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Preserve the source file and record identifiers, and keep per-row results for any write operation. Start with a reviewed pilot, reconcile partial success, and identify a recovery owner. A completed data job can still contain rejected rows or incorrect business mappings.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Matching Rules and review the available standard and custom rules. Choose matching criteria that represent the business identity rather than relying on one weak descriptive field.
  2. Create or adjust a supported custom matching rule when needed, using the available exact or fuzzy matching options. Review blank handling and test known duplicate and nonduplicate examples.
  3. Activate the matching rule according to the feature's requirements. Then open Duplicate Rules and create or edit a rule that references the intended matching rule.
  4. Configure create and edit behavior, such as alerting or blocking, and review record-level security behavior. Make the user message explain the corrective action without disclosing restricted data.
  5. Test manual creation, updates, and representative import or API paths. Include a legitimate similar record to ensure the rule does not prevent normal business work.
  6. Review activation and rule order, then roll out with a process for resolving flagged duplicates. Monitor rejected or alerted records before making the policy stricter.

Example

Two accounts with the same company name may be separate legal entities, while slightly different names can describe the same entity. The matching rule and blocking decision should reflect that distinction.

Verify the result

Confirm known duplicates are identified and valid similar records remain usable. Check the exact save action, message, and import behavior for the intended user population.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If duplicates pass through, inspect active rules, criteria, conditions, and the entry path. If too many records are blocked, examine matching strength, blanks, and rule conditions before disabling all duplicate management.

Limitations

A matching rule identifies candidates and a duplicate rule controls supported save behavior. Activating them does not automatically merge existing duplicates or replace a data-cleanup process.

Title: Merge Duplicate Accounts or Contacts
Summary: Consolidate supported duplicate records after reviewing the survivor, field values, and related information.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Consolidate supported duplicate records after reviewing the survivor, field values, and related information.

Before you begin

Confirm the records represent the same business entity and use a user authorized to merge them. Capture their IDs and a backup, and consult owners of external references before proceeding.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Preserve the source file and record identifiers, and keep per-row results for any write operation. Start with a reviewed pilot, reconcile partial success, and identify a recovery owner. A completed data job can still contain rejected rows or incorrect business mappings.

Steps

  1. Open the supported duplicate-review or merge interface for the object. Use identified duplicate candidates and verify each candidate against business identifiers rather than merging on a similar name alone.
  2. Select the intended surviving record and compare field values. Decide which values should remain, including owner, record type, external identifiers, and populated custom fields.
  3. Review related records and feature-specific merge considerations. Check integrations and references that store the IDs of records that will no longer be the survivor.
  4. Execute a small approved merge through the supported interface. Read confirmation messages carefully because a merge affects both field values and record relationships.
  5. Open the surviving record and inspect important related lists, ownership, sharing, and key fields. Reconcile the original IDs with the resulting record according to the integration design.
  6. Record the outcome and update duplicate-management rules or source-system mappings where necessary. Repeat only after the pilot proves the merge behaves as intended.

Example

Before merging two account records, determine which external customer key is authoritative. Keeping two conflicting source keys without a reconciliation decision can cause the next import to recreate the duplicate.

Verify the result

Confirm the surviving record contains the selected values and expected related information. Check that users and integrations resolve the intended entity and that the original duplicate is no longer an ordinary separate active record.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If merge controls are unavailable, inspect object support, permissions, sharing, and the current interface. If related data seems missing, investigate the object-specific merge behavior and retained IDs before performing another merge.

Limitations

Merge behavior varies by object and related feature. Do not treat merging as an ordinary deletion with guaranteed one-click reversal; review recovery and downstream references before the operation.

Title: Export a Data Backup Before a Bulk Change
Summary: Capture the records and relationships needed to investigate or reverse an approved data update.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Capture the records and relationships needed to investigate or reverse an approved data update.

Before you begin

Define the objects, fields, files, and relationships that must be preserved. Choose an approved storage location and a recovery owner before creating a potentially sensitive export.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Preserve the source file and record identifiers, and keep per-row results for any write operation. Start with a reviewed pilot, reconcile partial success, and identify a recovery owner. A completed data job can still contain rejected rows or incorrect business mappings.

Steps

  1. Determine whether Setup Data Export, Data Loader, or another approved export tool fits the recovery requirement. Check object coverage, available scheduling, and whether deleted records or files need separate treatment.
  2. For Setup Data Export, open the Data Export page and review the available export options. Select the relevant objects and file-related options when those are required and supported.
  3. For a targeted tool export, include record IDs, fields to be changed, and necessary relationship identifiers. Keep API field names and the target-org identity with the export.
  4. Run the export and obtain all generated files through the approved process. Record the extraction time and row counts so later comparisons use the same baseline.
  5. Open a sample in a safe inspection tool and verify identifiers, encoding, representative values, and relationship columns. Protect the original files from accidental spreadsheet conversion.
  6. Test a recovery approach in a test environment where appropriate. Confirm which data can be restored by update and which relationships, files, or generated values require a separate method.

Example

Before updating account classifications, export account IDs and the current classification values. A report containing only account names is not a reliable restoration mapping when names are duplicated.

Verify the result

Confirm the export includes the complete intended scope and usable record identifiers. Verify the files can be read and a representative recovery operation can map a row back to the correct record.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If an object is missing, inspect export coverage and permissions. If counts differ from expectations, inspect filters, record visibility, extraction timing, and whether the chosen tool includes deleted records.

Limitations

A data export is not a complete metadata backup or an automatic restore solution. Availability and scheduling depend on edition and feature support, and generated downloads can have limited availability.

Title: Restore an Accidentally Deleted Record
Summary: Use the Recycle Bin for supported recoverable records and verify related business information afterward.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Use the Recycle Bin for supported recoverable records and verify related business information afterward.

Before you begin

Collect the record type, name, ID if known, deletion time, and deleting user. Stop repeat deletions or source automation before restoring a record that could be removed again.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Preserve the source file and record identifiers, and keep per-row results for any write operation. Start with a reviewed pilot, reconcile partial success, and identify a recovery owner. A completed data job can still contain rejected rows or incorrect business mappings.

Steps

  1. Open Recycle Bin in Lightning Experience through the available navigation or App Launcher. Select the personal or organization scope you are authorized to inspect.
  2. Search for the intended record and compare its object, name, deletion information, and identifier. Do not restore several similar records merely because the exact original has not been identified.
  3. Select the recoverable record and choose Restore. Read any failure message about missing parents, duplicates, constraints, or permissions before retrying.
  4. Open the restored record in the intended app and inspect ownership, required relationships, related lists, and values important to the business process.
  5. Check reports, automation, and integrations that reference the record. A restored record may require business reconciliation even when the restore operation succeeds.
  6. Record the cause of deletion and fix the process that led to it. If the record is absent or no longer recoverable, use the approved backup-and-recovery procedure with the data owner.

Example

A deleted request can be restored while still recoverable in the Recycle Bin. If its related parent was also deleted, investigate the parent relationship and restore ordering rather than creating a replacement blindly.

Verify the result

Confirm the correct record is active again and authorized users can access it. Compare key fields and relationships with the backup or original task, and ensure it is not deleted again by the same process.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the record is missing, inspect the authorized scope, retention, and whether hard deletion or permanent removal occurred. If restore fails, resolve the named dependency or constraint instead of repeatedly clicking Restore.

Limitations

Recycle Bin recovery has retention and capacity limits and does not cover every deletion scenario. Hard-deleted or permanently removed data requires a different recovery strategy and may not be recoverable.

Title: Transfer Record Ownership in a Controlled Batch
Summary: Reassign records while reviewing sharing, related records, and operational responsibility.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Reassign records while reviewing sharing, related records, and operational responsibility.

Before you begin

Identify eligible source and destination owners, the exact object and record scope, and the reason for transfer. Export IDs and current owners and review related-record transfer behavior.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Preserve the source file and record identifiers, and keep per-row results for any write operation. Start with a reviewed pilot, reconcile partial success, and identify a recovery owner. A completed data job can still contain rejected rows or incorrect business mappings.

Steps

  1. Choose the supported tool for the scope: a record's Change Owner action, Setup Mass Transfer Records for supported objects, or an approved API update for a precise ID-based batch.
  2. Confirm the destination user is active and eligible to own the object. For a queue, verify the object supports queue ownership and the queue is configured for it.
  3. Define the selection narrowly and compare the candidate count with the approved scope. Review open and closed records separately if different teams should retain historical responsibility.
  4. Read all related-record and notification options offered by the transfer tool. Ownership of children, manual shares, teams, and access can be affected differently for different objects.
  5. Transfer a small pilot and inspect the resulting owner, sharing, related records, and notifications. Check that automation has not reassigned the record immediately afterward.
  6. Process the remaining approved scope and reconcile every record ID with its new owner. Keep the old-owner mapping and verify the recipient's work lists and reporting.

Example

When a representative leaves, transfer the approved open opportunities rather than every historical record by default. Account ownership and opportunity ownership may need separate review depending on the selected transfer method.

Verify the result

Compare pre- and post-transfer owner IDs and confirm the count matches the intended batch. Test destination-owner access and inspect any related records included by the transfer options.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If ownership reverts, inspect assignment rules, flows, and other automation. If users lose access, inspect owner-based sharing, hierarchy, teams, and manual-share behavior before broadening organization-wide defaults.

Limitations

Ownership transfer can change record access and notifications. Tool options and related-record behavior vary by object, so do not assume a parent transfer moves every dependent record.

Title: Choose the Right Flow Type and Timing
Summary: Select a Flow entry point and execution timing that fit the business event and required work.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Select a Flow entry point and execution timing that fit the business event and required work.

Before you begin

Write the triggering event, required inputs, records to change, and desired outcome in plain language. Inventory existing automation on the object before adding another flow.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review existing automation and execution context before activation. Use disposable test records and controlled notification recipients, and inspect side effects as well as the highlighted flow path. Keep a known prior version and reconcile committed work separately from version changes.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Flows and review existing definitions related to the requirement. Check whether the task extends an existing design rather than creating a second competing automation.
  2. Choose a Screen Flow when a user must provide information through screens. Choose a record-triggered flow when a supported record event should start the automation without interactive input.
  3. For record-triggered work, use before-save timing for supported changes to the triggering record. Choose after-save timing when the requirement includes related records or supported actions unavailable before save.
  4. Consider scheduled-triggered flows for a recurring query-driven job and scheduled paths for a future action associated with a qualifying record event. These are different scheduling models.
  5. Define entry conditions and repeat-execution behavior before drawing elements. Decide what should happen on create, update, and an update that leaves the record already qualifying.
  6. Build a small test version and compare the result with the written requirement. Review execution context, error handling, and all existing automation before activation.

Example

Setting a default classification on the triggering request can fit before-save timing. Creating a follow-up task after a request is approved generally requires after-save work instead.

Verify the result

Trace one realistic event from entry through outcome and confirm the chosen flow supports every required element. Check a nonqualifying event and an update that should not repeat the action.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If an element is unavailable, confirm the flow type and timing rather than searching indefinitely for it. If behavior repeats, inspect entry criteria and existing automation before adding another decision branch.

Limitations

Flow type and execution context affect behavior and access. Do not choose system-level execution as a shortcut around an unresolved business-permission requirement.

Title: Build a Before-Save Flow to Set a Field
Summary: Update a value on the triggering record without performing a separate update to that same record.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Update a value on the triggering record without performing a separate update to that same record.

Before you begin

Choose a supported object and a deterministic field rule. Define when the field may be set and whether a user-supplied value should be preserved.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review existing automation and execution context before activation. Use disposable test records and controlled notification recipients, and inspect side effects as well as the highlighted flow path. Keep a known prior version and reconcile committed work separately from version changes.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Flows and create a Record-Triggered Flow. Select the object, triggering events, and entry conditions that represent the business rule.
  2. Choose Fast Field Updates for before-save timing. Review which elements are supported and confirm the task only needs changes appropriate to that timing.
  3. Add a Decision when different input states require different outcomes. Include an explicit path for records that should keep their current value.
  4. Use an Assignment to set the appropriate field on the triggering record variable, such as a field under $Record. Avoid adding a separate Update Records operation for the same triggering record.
  5. Save with a descriptive API name and version description, then debug representative inputs in the test environment. Check nulls, existing values, and update events as well as new records.
  6. Activate only after checking other flows and validation rules on the object. Create or edit a real test record through the intended interface to verify the saved result.

Example

If a new request has no priority and its category is Routine, a before-save assignment can supply the approved default. A deliberately entered user priority should remain unchanged when the business rule says to preserve it.

Verify the result

Confirm the stored field value matches the rule after a valid save and a nonqualifying record is unchanged. Include a user-supplied value and a validation-failure case.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the value is overwritten, inspect entry conditions, assignment logic, and later automation. If the flow never starts, verify the active version, object, event, and condition transition selected in Start.

Limitations

Before-save timing is for supported fast changes to the triggering record. Use a different timing or flow design for related-record creation, interactive screens, or unsupported external actions.

Title: Create a Related Record with an After-Save Flow
Summary: Create one related business record when a qualifying parent event occurs.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Create one related business record when a qualifying parent event occurs.

Before you begin

Identify the source event, related object, required fields, ownership, and rule for preventing repeat creation. Review existing automation that may already create the related record.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review existing automation and execution context before activation. Use disposable test records and controlled notification recipients, and inspect side effects as well as the highlighted flow path. Keep a known prior version and reconcile committed work separately from version changes.

Steps

  1. Create a Record-Triggered Flow for the source object and choose Actions and Related Records. Set the create or update event and narrow entry conditions.
  2. For a transition such as first becoming Approved, use supported entry and prior-value logic so later unrelated edits do not create the same follow-up repeatedly.
  3. Determine whether an existing related record should be reused or block creation. Add a supported lookup and Decision when a durable duplicate-prevention check is required.
  4. Add Create Records with the target object and populate required fields, source-record relationship, owner, and any approved defaults. Use actual field references and supported picklist values.
  5. Add a fault connector where supported and route failures to an appropriate handling path. Keep operational details out of user-visible messages and avoid recursive error-handling designs.
  6. Debug qualifying, nonqualifying, repeated-update, and missing-data scenarios. Activate the tested version and run the intended record-save path in the test org.

Example

A request becoming Approved can create one follow-up task related to that request. Editing the request's description afterward should not create another task unless the business process explicitly requires one.

Verify the result

Confirm the related record is created once with the correct parent, owner, required values, and access. Repeat an unrelated update and inspect the target object for unintended duplicates.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If creation fails, inspect required fields, validation rules, ownership eligibility, and the fault details. If duplicates appear, inspect repeat-entry behavior and concurrency assumptions before simply adding another Get Records element.

Limitations

After-save flows can interact with other automation and trigger further saves. A lookup-based duplicate check alone does not establish a universal concurrency-safe uniqueness guarantee.

Title: Create a Screen Flow for Guided Data Entry
Summary: Guide users through a focused task with clear inputs and a controlled save operation.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Guide users through a focused task with clear inputs and a controlled save operation.

Before you begin

Define the user task, input fields, target records, and cancellation behavior. Decide whether the flow should receive a record ID from its launch context.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review existing automation and execution context before activation. Use disposable test records and controlled notification recipients, and inspect side effects as well as the highlighted flow path. Keep a known prior version and reconcile committed work separately from version changes.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Flows and create a Screen Flow. Add a Screen with labeled components for the required user inputs and help text that explains unfamiliar values.
  2. Create resources with appropriate data types and supported input settings. If the launch surface supplies a record ID, define the expected input variable and make it available for input.
  3. Add Decisions and data operations needed to validate context and save the intended record. Check that a supplied record ID actually refers to the supported object and task.
  4. Review the flow's configured execution context and permissions. Use the narrowest context that satisfies the design and do not expose protected information through screen defaults or messages.
  5. Add supported fault handling and a useful completion screen. Make clear when data has been saved, especially if the flow crosses multiple screens or transaction boundaries.
  6. Debug normal, missing-input, invalid-record, cancellation, and failure scenarios. Activate the tested version and distribute it through an approved record page, action, or other supported surface.

Example

A request-entry flow can ask for category and description, confirm the details, and then create a request. Its launch context should determine whether the user chooses an account or receives a validated account ID.

Verify the result

Run the activated flow as the intended user and inspect the created record. Check validation messages, parent relationships, cancellation behavior, and what happens if the same task is submitted again.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If input is missing, inspect the variable name, type, and launch mapping. If a save fails, inspect execution context, required fields, validation rules, and the specific failed element.

Limitations

Screen navigation does not guarantee rollback of every earlier data operation. Design save points and cancellation carefully rather than promising that leaving a flow always removes all prior changes.

Title: Control Record-Triggered Flow Entry Conditions
Summary: Prevent unnecessary runs and repeated side effects by defining exactly when a flow should start.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Prevent unnecessary runs and repeated side effects by defining exactly when a flow should start.

Before you begin

Write the qualifying state and the transition into that state. Decide whether actions should run on every qualifying update or only when a record newly meets the conditions.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review existing automation and execution context before activation. Use disposable test records and controlled notification recipients, and inspect side effects as well as the highlighted flow path. Keep a known prior version and reconcile committed work separately from version changes.

Steps

  1. Open the record-triggered flow in Flow Builder and inspect Start. Confirm the object, create or update events, condition requirements, and timing are all relevant to the task.
  2. Enter the narrowest correct entry criteria using supported conditions or a formula. Include blank handling and condition logic explicitly when several fields determine eligibility.
  3. For update events, choose the supported option for every qualifying update or only when the record is updated to meet the conditions. Match that choice to the required business event.
  4. Use supported current and prior values when the requirement concerns a specific field change. Do not assume a condition such as Status equals Approved means Status changed to Approved.
  5. Review downstream updates that can cause the flow or other automation to execute again. Avoid loops in which two automations repeatedly change each other's entry fields.
  6. Test create, false-to-true transition, true-to-true update, and true-to-false transition. Include a record that changes one condition but still qualifies through another branch.

Example

If Category is Hardware OR Priority is High, changing Category while Priority remains High may leave the whole condition true. A flow configured only for newly qualifying records should be tested against that combined logic.

Verify the result

Record the expected number of executions for each test scenario and compare actual field changes or related records. Confirm an unrelated edit does not repeat a one-time business action.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If the flow does not rerun, inspect whether the overall condition was already true. If it runs too often, inspect the event selection, update behavior, prior-value logic, and automation that changes the same record.

Limitations

Different flow timings and asynchronous paths have different supported operators. Entry filtering reduces work but does not by itself establish duplicate-proof processing for every concurrent event.

Title: Debug a Flow Before Activation
Summary: Inspect a controlled execution path and compare its values with explicit expected results.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Inspect a controlled execution path and compare its values with explicit expected results.

Before you begin

Use a test org and disposable records with known inputs. List the flow's paths, side effects, and expected outcomes before starting a debug session.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review existing automation and execution context before activation. Use disposable test records and controlled notification recipients, and inspect side effects as well as the highlighted flow path. Keep a known prior version and reconcile committed work separately from version changes.

Steps

  1. Open the intended flow version in Flow Builder and select Debug. Confirm you are testing the version you plan to activate rather than assuming the latest version is already active.
  2. Configure the supported debug inputs, record, event, and user options. Read available rollback or simulation controls for this flow type instead of assuming every debug run is nonmutating.
  3. Run the test and inspect the executed path, resource values, Decisions, and data-operation results. Compare each important branch with the expected result written before the run.
  4. Repeat with blank values, a nonqualifying case, and a known failure condition. For record-triggered flows, test relevant create and update transitions through their supported debug options.
  5. Use supported flow tests for repeatable assertions when available and appropriate. Save meaningful cases for each important path rather than only checking that the flow opens.
  6. After successful debugging, test the activated flow through its actual launch path in the test org. Include surrounding automation because an isolated debug result may not reproduce every runtime interaction.

Example

A debug run that takes the expected Decision branch can still reveal an incorrect owner ID passed to Create Records. Inspect resource values and saved outcomes instead of judging only the highlighted path.

Verify the result

Confirm each planned scenario produces its expected branch, values, and record changes. Retain the input record or synthetic data description so a later flow version can repeat the same test.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If debug and runtime differ, compare active versions, execution users, input mappings, entry events, and surrounding automation. Check whether debug simulation or rollback settings changed which operations actually committed.

Limitations

Debugging can execute real operations depending on flow type and options. A successful single debug run is not proof that all paths, permissions, scheduled work, or integrations behave correctly.

Title: Handle Flow Faults with Actionable Information
Summary: Provide controlled recovery or escalation when a supported Flow element fails.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Provide controlled recovery or escalation when a supported Flow element fails.

Before you begin

Identify data operations and actions that can fail, the people who should be notified, and whether the flow is interactive or runs in the background.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review existing automation and execution context before activation. Use disposable test records and controlled notification recipients, and inspect side effects as well as the highlighted flow path. Keep a known prior version and reconcile committed work separately from version changes.

Steps

  1. Open the flow and inspect elements with supported fault connectors, such as data operations and actions. List likely failures including validation errors, missing references, and unavailable services.
  2. Connect each relevant fault path to a deliberate handling sequence. For a screen flow, provide an understandable message and next step without exposing internal IDs, credentials, or raw technical details.
  3. For background work, choose an approved notification or logging mechanism and capture useful context such as flow name, version, element, record reference, and failure category. Protect sensitive data in diagnostics.
  4. Decide whether a failure should stop the operation, permit a partial outcome, or create a follow-up task. Review transaction behavior so a handled fault does not silently leave users believing all work succeeded.
  5. Test a controlled failure and confirm both the user experience and the administrator's diagnostic evidence. Make sure the handling path does not trigger the same failure repeatedly.
  6. Review ordinary success cases after adding fault handling. Document who owns investigation and how to reconcile a failed run before retrying an operation with possible side effects.

Example

If creating a follow-up record fails validation, a screen flow can tell the user the task was not completed and provide a support reference. A diagnostic record should avoid copying an entire sensitive form submission.

Verify the result

Confirm an induced error reaches the intended handling path and produces the promised outcome. Inspect committed records to verify that the message accurately describes any partial work.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If no diagnostic appears, inspect whether the failing element supports the connector and whether logging was rolled back or failed itself. If users receive duplicate alerts, inspect retries and recursive automation.

Limitations

Fault connectors do not catch every platform limit or failure mode. Logging inside a transaction can also be rolled back, so choose an operational design that matches the required reliability.

Title: Schedule a Future Action from a Record-Triggered Flow
Summary: Run a supported follow-up after a qualifying record event or a record-based time source.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Run a supported follow-up after a qualifying record event or a record-based time source.

Before you begin

Define the time source, offset, eligibility at execution, and duplicate-prevention rule. Confirm the organization's Default Workflow User and review inactive-user handling.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review existing automation and execution context before activation. Use disposable test records and controlled notification recipients, and inspect side effects as well as the highlighted flow path. Keep a known prior version and reconcile committed work separately from version changes.

Steps

  1. Create or open an after-save record-triggered flow optimized for Actions and Related Records. Configure supported entry conditions and transition behavior for the intended scheduled action.
  2. In Start, add a Scheduled Path with a descriptive label. Choose the supported time source, such as the triggering event or an eligible record field, and specify the offset.
  3. Define the path's work and review whether record conditions should be checked again before acting. Design the action to avoid unwanted duplicates when a date or eligibility changes.
  4. In Setup, review Process Automation Settings and the Default Workflow User. Confirm the designated user is active and appropriate for the organization's automation policy.
  5. Test scheduling with a near-term disposable record and inspect the available time-based workflow monitoring view. Include a changed time-source value and a record that no longer qualifies.
  6. Monitor the action when its scheduled time arrives, then verify the resulting records or notifications. Document the consequences of deactivating the flow while work is waiting.

Example

A request can schedule a reminder relative to its planned review date. Updating that date may affect future scheduling, so the design should specify whether another reminder is legitimate after a previous one already ran.

Verify the result

Confirm the item is scheduled relative to the intended source and performs the correct action once eligible. Test the changed-date and no-longer-qualifying scenarios rather than only the initial schedule.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If no work is queued, inspect supported entry settings, time source, active version, and whether the qualifying transition occurred. If work disappears or fails to execute, review record changes, deactivation, and available fault information.

Limitations

A scheduled path differs from a scheduled-triggered flow. Exact execution timing and batching are platform-controlled, and pending-work behavior must be reviewed before changing or deactivating the flow.

Title: Activate a Flow Version and Restore a Previous Version
Summary: Promote a tested Flow version and verify which definition starts new executions.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Promote a tested Flow version and verify which definition starts new executions.

Before you begin

Have a tested candidate version, a known prior version, and an impact review for waiting or running work. Record the intended activation time and the acceptance checks.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Review existing automation and execution context before activation. Use disposable test records and controlled notification recipients, and inspect side effects as well as the highlighted flow path. Keep a known prior version and reconcile committed work separately from version changes.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Flows and inspect the definition's versions. Compare the candidate's description, type, and changes with the version currently marked active.
  2. Open and validate the candidate in Flow Builder. Resolve validation warnings or errors relevant to activation and confirm required dependencies exist in the target environment.
  3. Activate the approved version through the available version controls. Check the definition afterward to confirm which version is active rather than relying only on the editor's open tab.
  4. Run a controlled new execution through the actual launch path and verify expected records and notifications. Check scheduled or asynchronous effects using the relevant monitoring tools.
  5. If the candidate fails acceptance, inspect the prior compatible version and activate it through the supported controls. Confirm new executions now use the intended previous definition.
  6. Reconcile records and external side effects produced by the candidate. Monitor paused interviews and pending work separately because changing the active version is not equivalent to reversing completed transactions.

Example

If a new flow creates tasks with the wrong priority, restoring the earlier active version can protect future runs. Tasks already created with the wrong value still require an explicit data correction.

Verify the result

Confirm the active marker and test a new execution after both activation and any restoration. Compare results with the acceptance scenarios and check outstanding work that began under another version.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If behavior still appears old, inspect the launch surface, flow API name, active version, and existing interview. If activation fails, resolve the named dependency or validation issue instead of deleting prior versions.

Limitations

Version activation governs future launches according to the flow's runtime behavior. It does not undo previously committed records, sent messages, or every already-running or waiting interview.

Title: Configure Lead Statuses and a Lead Process
Summary: Offer an approved lead qualification lifecycle through status values and a record-type lead process.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Offer an approved lead qualification lifecycle through status values and a record-type lead process.

Before you begin

Agree the business meaning of each status and which statuses represent conversion. Inventory automation, reports, integrations, and existing leads that depend on current status values.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Object Manager, select Lead, and inspect the Status field in Fields & Relationships. Review active values and their converted-status designation.
  2. Add or adjust only the approved statuses and preserve stable API values where integrations depend on them. Plan a separate data migration before replacing values used by existing records.
  3. In Setup, open Lead Processes and create or edit the process that represents the intended qualification path. Include the approved subset of available statuses.
  4. Open Lead record types and associate the intended lead process. Review availability, defaults, and assigned page layouts for the users who create or update those leads.
  5. Test a new lead and an existing lead with each relevant record type. Verify status choices and the conversion experience without assuming all statuses are interchangeable.
  6. Update training and report definitions to match the agreed lifecycle. Review assignment rules and flows that depend on a status label or API value before activating the change.

Example

A partner lead process can use a smaller qualification path than a direct-sales process. Both can draw from the org's lead statuses while exposing only the choices approved for their respective record types.

Verify the result

Confirm available status choices match the process for each record type and the expected converted statuses are usable during conversion. Check an existing record as well as a new one.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a status is missing, inspect its active state and the lead process associated with the record type. If reporting changes unexpectedly, inspect replaced values and filters that use old status names.

Limitations

Lead processes govern supported status choices; they do not grant record visibility or automatically convert leads. Conversion still requires the appropriate permissions and valid target data.

Title: Route Leads with an Assignment Rule
Summary: Assign incoming leads to the intended user or queue using ordered, testable routing criteria.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Assign incoming leads to the intended user or queue using ordered, testable routing criteria.

Before you begin

Define routing criteria, precedence, and a fallback owner. Confirm queue support and owner eligibility, and identify which creation paths should invoke assignment rules.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Agree process definitions with sales operations and test using a representative sales user. Check record types, ownership, and automation as well as screen choices. Avoid changing live status meanings or source identifiers without reviewing reporting and integration consumers.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Lead Assignment Rules and review the current rule and active configuration. Plan changes within the intended active rule rather than assuming several active rules run together.
  2. Create or edit the rule entries with clear sort order. Put more specific matches before broader conditions and document the first-match behavior expected by the routing design.
  3. For each entry, configure criteria and select an eligible user or queue. Review any supported email notification template and confirm recipients before testing notifications.
  4. Set the approved active rule and review relevant lead defaults. Check whether each manual, web, import, or API entry path actually requests assignment-rule processing.
  5. Create pilot leads that match each entry, overlap multiple entries, and match none. Include the real creation path so a successful direct test does not mask a missing assignment option in an integration.
  6. Inspect Owner after save and after subsequent automation. Record which entry should win for overlapping criteria and document ownership of future routing changes.

Example

A high-priority regional lead should match the specific regional priority entry before a general region entry. A broad rule placed first can capture the lead before the specific entry is considered.

Verify the result

Confirm owner IDs for every test case, including the fallback. Check queue membership and notification results and verify that a later flow does not immediately replace the assigned owner.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If assignment is ignored, check the active rule, entry order, criteria, and whether the save path invokes it. If the owner changes again, inspect flows and other automation rather than continually rearranging rule entries.

Limitations

Assignment-rule execution is entry-path dependent, especially for API operations. A configured rule does not guarantee that every edit of every lead will invoke the same routing behavior.

Title: Capture Leads with Web-to-Lead
Summary: Generate a supported website lead form and test its submission, ownership, and required data.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Generate a supported website lead form and test its submission, ownership, and required data.

  2. Use the form-generation tool to select the lead fields and the intended return location. Include only fields the organization needs to collect through this public channel.
  3. Review the generated form with the website team. Add approved labeling, accessibility, privacy information, and supported spam protection while preserving required Salesforce submission fields.
  4. Validate the form first on a controlled test page. Use the available debugging options only for testing and remove test-only behavior before public deployment.
  5. Submit a synthetic lead and inspect its stored values, owner, status, and source classification. Test assignment and response behavior through this actual intake path.
  6. Confirm validation failures and operational monitoring with the website and sales teams. Publish the reviewed form through the website's normal release process and monitor initial submissions.

Example

A contact-us form can populate Lead Source consistently and request a business email and company name. A new validation rule that requires an uncollected field can prevent the form from producing usable leads.

Verify the result

Submit valid and incomplete synthetic examples and verify the resulting leads and monitoring behavior. Check required fields, spam protection, duplicate handling, owner routing, and the return-page experience.

If no lead appears, inspect form submission fields, required values, validation rules, duplicate rules, limits, and available error notifications. Check whether the form still targets the intended org after environment changes.

Generated form HTML is a starting point rather than a complete website security or consent design. Web-to-Lead has platform limits and does not replace a monitored integration for every intake requirement.

Title: Map Custom Fields for Lead Conversion
Summary: Carry approved custom lead data into supported account, contact, or opportunity fields during conversion.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Carry approved custom lead data into supported account, contact, or opportunity fields during conversion.

Before you begin

Identify the source custom lead fields and compatible target fields. Define what should happen when conversion uses an existing target record that already contains data.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

  2. Select the intended account, contact, or opportunity destination fields through the supported mapping interface. Check field-type compatibility and size before selecting a target.
  3. Create missing target fields only through a separately reviewed schema change. Confirm the target field has the intended business meaning rather than mapping to a merely similar label.
  4. Save and test conversion into new target records with distinct sample values. Include a scenario where the user chooses not to create an opportunity.
  5. Test conversion against an existing account or contact with populated values. Inspect supported overwrite and preservation behavior instead of assuming the lead always replaces existing target data.
  6. Review validation rules, record types, permissions, and automation on the target objects. Document mappings for import and integration owners so source fields retain consistent meanings.

A lead's custom onboarding-region field can map to a compatible contact field. The business must decide how to handle an existing contact with a different region rather than treating conversion as an unrestricted overwrite.

Verify the result

Standard lead fields use Salesforce's standard conversion mappings. Custom field mappings do not by themselves control duplicate selection, ownership, every overwrite rule, or target-object automation.

Title: Convert a Qualified Lead
Summary: Create or select the right account and contact and optionally create an opportunity during lead conversion.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Create or select the right account and contact and optionally create an opportunity during lead conversion.

Before you begin

Confirm the lead meets the business qualification criteria and the user can convert it. Review possible duplicates and required target-object information before starting.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Agree process definitions with sales operations and test using a representative sales user. Check record types, ownership, and automation as well as screen choices. Avoid changing live status meanings or source identifiers without reviewing reporting and integration consumers.

Steps

  1. Open the lead in the intended app and review company, contact details, qualification status, and custom fields used during conversion. Correct missing source data before selecting Convert.
  2. In the conversion dialog, review suggested existing accounts and contacts. Choose the correct existing entity when appropriate rather than creating another record solely because it is the default option.
  3. Decide whether an opportunity is required now and use the supported option accordingly. Confirm the opportunity name and other values presented for the sales process.

  5. Complete conversion and inspect the resulting account, contact, and optional opportunity. Verify custom field mappings and important related information rather than assuming the success message covers every business requirement.
  6. Record the outcome and move to the target records for ongoing work. Resolve any validation or duplicate conflict through the organization's process instead of repeatedly creating near-identical entities.

A qualified lead for an existing customer can convert into that account and an appropriate contact, with an opportunity only when a genuine deal should be tracked. Conversion does not always require creating a new account.

Confirm the lead is marked converted and references the intended target records. Check ownership, mapped fields, record types, and any expected opportunity or follow-up automation.

Conversion changes the lead lifecycle and is not a casual reversible edit. Converted-lead visibility and editing require appropriate capabilities, so validate the target choices carefully before completing the action.

Title: Configure Opportunity Stages and Sales Processes

Align opportunity stage choices, probabilities, and forecast meanings with an approved sales lifecycle.

A renewal process can have fewer stages than a new-business process while both use the organization's stage definitions. Record types associate each process with its intended opportunity population.

Verify the result

Confirm available stages and closed-won or closed-lost meanings for each record type. Check probabilities, forecast categories, and reports with known sample amounts and dates.

Title: Guide Users with Path
Summary: Display key fields and stage-specific guidance for a supported object and picklist process.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Display key fields and stage-specific guidance for a supported object and picklist process.

An opportunity Path can show qualification questions at an early stage and contracting guidance later. It helps users understand the process without making the guidance itself an enforced validation rule.

Verify the result

Open records with the intended record type and confirm the right Path and guidance appear. Test a permitted stage transition and inspect the stored picklist value after save.

Title: Set Up Products and Price Books
Summary: Make approved products and prices available for opportunity line items.

Title: Configure Campaign Member Statuses
Summary: Track meaningful participation and response outcomes for a specific campaign.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Track meaningful participation and response outcomes for a specific campaign.

Before you begin

Agree the campaign's participation lifecycle and which statuses count as a response. Confirm Campaign access and the user capabilities required to maintain campaign configuration.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Agree process definitions with sales operations and test using a representative sales user. Check record types, ownership, and automation as well as screen choices. Avoid changing live status meanings or source identifiers without reviewing reporting and integration consumers.

Steps

  1. Open the campaign and inspect its Campaign Member Statuses related information. Add the related list or supported page component if the assigned page does not show it.
  2. Review the current status values and default status. Choose labels that represent this campaign's actual interactions, such as Invited, Registered, and Attended where those are appropriate.
  3. Add or edit supported statuses and set Responded according to the agreed measurement definition. The response flag should reflect a business decision rather than merely how positive a label sounds.
  4. Select the intended default for newly added members. Review existing members and integration mappings before deleting or replacing a status already in use.
  5. Add a small set of test leads or contacts as campaign members and apply each status. Check campaign response metrics and reports against those known inputs.
  6. Document the status model for campaign operations and connected marketing tools. Review cloned campaigns to confirm they carry the intended configuration rather than assuming every creation route copies it.

Example

For an event campaign, Registered and Attended can both count as responses if that is the agreed metric. For another campaign, the same labels may require a different measurement definition.

Verify the result

Confirm new members receive the intended default and response counts change according to the Responded flags. Compare campaign reports with the exact test members and their statuses.

If an import rejects a status, inspect the target campaign's available member statuses and the integration mapping. If response totals look wrong, inspect Responded settings and report filters before changing member records.

Limitations

Campaign member status is participation data for a campaign. It is distinct from the Campaign record's own Status and does not automatically describe every opportunity attribution or marketing-consent requirement.

A billing case process can use a different supported subset of statuses from technical support. The record type chooses the relevant support process, while the underlying status definition determines whether a case is closed.
