Title: Route Cases with an Assignment Rule
Summary: Send cases to the right support user or queue through ordered criteria and a verified intake path.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Send cases to the right support user or queue through ordered criteria and a verified intake path.

Before you begin

Define case-routing priorities and a fallback owner. Confirm queue membership, case permissions, and which intake paths should invoke the assignment rule.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Agree the support or content lifecycle with its business owner and test with synthetic customer information. Verify routing, publication, and visibility independently. A saved configuration or a success message does not prove that the intended support audience can use the result.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Case Assignment Rules and inspect the current active configuration. Identify the intended rule and existing entries before making changes.
  2. Create or edit entries with explicit sort order and criteria. Place specific conditions before general ones so an early broad match does not capture work intended for a specialist queue.
  3. Choose an eligible user or case queue for each entry and configure supported notification options. Verify that queue members can access and work the cases.
  4. Activate the approved rule and review default case ownership and applicable support settings. Check manual, web, email, and API intake behavior separately.
  5. Create synthetic cases for each route, an overlapping match, and a no-match case through the actual intake path. For API-based tests, confirm the client explicitly invokes the intended assignment behavior.
  6. Inspect ownership after save and after other automation completes. Document the routing matrix and the team responsible for ongoing maintenance.

Example

An urgent technical case can route to a specialist queue before a general Technical entry is considered. The fallback should still assign a usable owner when no specialist condition matches.

Verify the result

Compare expected and actual owners for every pilot case. Check notifications, queue membership, and the ability of a queue member to accept and update the case.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If routing is ignored, inspect active state, sort order, criteria, and the intake's assignment-rule option. If ownership changes again, investigate flows and other automation instead of modifying the rule repeatedly.

Limitations

Assignment rules are not a complete workforce-routing system. A queue assignment does not automatically configure Omni-Channel capacity, presence, or push routing.

Title: Send Case Acknowledgments with Auto-Response Rules
Summary: Send an appropriate acknowledgment for supported case intake events using approved criteria and templates.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Send an appropriate acknowledgment for supported case intake events using approved criteria and templates.

Before you begin

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Agree the support or content lifecycle with its business owner and test with synthetic customer information. Verify routing, publication, and visibility independently. A saved configuration or a success message does not prove that the intended support audience can use the result.

Steps

  1. Prepare an email template supported by case auto-response rules. Include useful acknowledgment information and avoid exposing fields that should not be emailed to the requester.
  2. In Setup, open Case Auto-Response Rules and inspect the active rule. Create or edit the intended rule and define ordered entries for the supported intake scenarios.
  3. Configure each entry's criteria, approved sender details, and template. Review the first-match ordering so a general template does not precede a more specific language or product route.
  4. Activate the approved configuration and review channel defaults, especially email-based intake that may have additional acknowledgment settings. Prevent overlapping features from sending duplicate messages.
  5. Submit a synthetic case through the actual channel with a controlled recipient mailbox. Inspect the case, sender, template merge values, and received message.
  6. Test an unmatched case and a case without a usable recipient address. Document which feature sends the acknowledgment for each channel and how failures are monitored.

Example

A web support form can send a product-specific acknowledgment while a general entry covers other submissions. The email should confirm receipt without promising a response time the support process does not enforce.

Verify the result

Confirm one intended acknowledgment reaches the controlled recipient with correct merge fields and sender information. Check routing separately because an email response does not prove the case owner is correct.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If no message arrives, inspect rule matching, activation, channel behavior, recipient address, sender verification, and delivery logs. If two messages arrive, inspect both rule-based and channel-specific response settings.

Limitations

Auto-response rules apply to supported submission behavior rather than every case edit. An acknowledgment is not an entitlement, an escalation rule, or a guarantee of email delivery.

Title: Escalate Unresolved Cases with Escalation Rules
Summary: Reassign or notify on qualifying unresolved cases using an approved aging clock and support schedule.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Reassign or notify on qualifying unresolved cases using an approved aging clock and support schedule.

Before you begin

Define the escalation threshold, aging basis, business-hours schedule, recipients, and expected action. Review current rules and avoid implying a contractual SLA unless the broader service design supports it.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Agree the support or content lifecycle with its business owner and test with synthetic customer information. Verify routing, publication, and visibility independently. A saved configuration or a success message does not prove that the intended support audience can use the result.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Escalation Rules and inspect the active rule and ordered entries. Identify the intended case population and how specific entries should take precedence.
  2. Create or edit an entry with explicit criteria and the appropriate business-hours behavior. Select the intended aging basis offered by the feature rather than assuming the clock always starts from the same event.
  3. Add escalation actions with the approved time threshold, new owner if applicable, and notification recipients. Confirm the selected user or queue is eligible to receive the cases.
  4. Review holidays and the referenced business-hours schedule. Check whether a case leaving the qualifying state or being closed should change the escalation outcome.
  5. Activate and test with disposable cases and practical test thresholds. Include working time, a closed period, and a case resolved before escalation.
  6. Inspect resulting owner changes and messages, then restore production thresholds before rollout. Document who monitors escalated work so escalation does not merely move cases into another unattended queue.

Example

An unresolved high-priority case can escalate after the agreed amount of support time. A holiday associated with the schedule should be considered when verifying when the escalation is expected.

Verify the result

Confirm the escalation clock, owner change, and notification behavior with known test cases. Verify a closed or nonqualifying case does not receive the unintended escalation.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If timing is wrong, inspect the aging basis, schedule, holidays, entry criteria, and actual case history. If routing changes afterward, inspect assignment and flow automation that may alter the owner.

Limitations

Escalation rules differ from entitlement milestones and external SLA measurement. Platform scheduling is not an exact-to-the-second guarantee, so validate the behavior required by the support process.

Title: Set Up Email-to-Case Routing
Summary: Turn messages sent to an approved support address into cases and test the complete mail route.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Turn messages sent to an approved support address into cases and test the complete mail route.

Before you begin

Confirm the supported Email-to-Case mode, mailbox ownership, verification access, and security approval. Plan sender behavior, case ownership, attachments, spam handling, and duplicate acknowledgment prevention.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Agree the support or content lifecycle with its business owner and test with synthetic customer information. Verify routing, publication, and visibility independently. A saved configuration or a success message does not prove that the intended support audience can use the result.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Email-to-Case and review the enablement and mode options available in the org. Select the approved supported approach rather than mixing agent-based and on-demand procedures.
  2. Create or review a routing address for the business support mailbox. Configure supported defaults such as owner, priority, origin, and record type according to the intake design.
  3. Complete the routing-address verification process and obtain the Salesforce-generated service address where applicable. Keep that generated address in the controlled mailbox configuration rather than inventing it.
  4. With the mail administrator, configure forwarding from the approved support mailbox to the verified service address. Review loops, unwanted senders, and mail policies before enabling broad traffic.
  5. Send a synthetic external message through the actual public support address. Inspect the case, email record, attachments, ownership, acknowledgment, and any assignment behavior.
  6. Reply through the intended agent experience and test a customer reply. Verify threading and monitoring so follow-up messages attach to the expected case rather than silently creating unrelated cases.

Example

Testing a message sent directly to a generated service address does not prove that the public support mailbox forwards correctly. Run the full customer-to-mailbox-to-Salesforce path before release.

Verify the result

Confirm a new message creates the intended case and a reply follows the designed threading behavior. Check attachments, owner, origin, sender identity, and that no email loop or duplicate response occurs.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If no case appears, inspect verification, forwarding, mailbox rules, limits, and error notifications. If replies create new cases, investigate current threading behavior and mail-header preservation with the mail team.

Limitations

Email-to-Case depends on both Salesforce and mail-system configuration and has message and attachment limits. It does not independently establish spam filtering, customer identity, or a complete email retention policy.

Title: Capture Support Requests with Web-to-Case
Summary: Generate a supported web case form and test case creation through the website intake path.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Generate a supported web case form and test case creation through the website intake path.

Title: Give Authors and Readers Appropriate Knowledge Access
Summary: Separate article-reading access from authoring, publishing, and broader administration capabilities.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Separate article-reading access from authoring, publishing, and broader administration capabilities.

Before you begin

Confirm Lightning Knowledge is already enabled and identify the user's product entitlements. Define separate reader, author, reviewer, and publisher responsibilities before assigning permissions.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Agree the support or content lifecycle with its business owner and test with synthetic customer information. Verify routing, publication, and visibility independently. A saved configuration or a success message does not prove that the intended support audience can use the result.

Steps

  1. In Setup, inspect the user's license and Knowledge-related entitlement or feature-user setting as applicable. Confirm the organization supports the requested role before changing permissions.
  2. Review the Knowledge object and article-field permissions in the appropriate profile and permission sets. Grant readers the access needed to read approved content and authors only the editing capabilities their role requires.
  3. Review article-management and publication-related permissions separately. Do not give every author unrestricted publishing or administrative capabilities simply to make a missing action appear.
  4. Add Knowledge to the intended app navigation and review article page layouts. UI availability helps users find the feature but does not grant underlying permissions.
  5. Test a published article as a reader and a draft as an author. Check publication state, language, channel visibility, and data-category visibility where configured.
  6. Test a denied action such as a reader attempting to edit or publish. Document the content owner and the workflow for requesting new author or publisher access.

Example

A support reader can need access to published internal articles while an author drafts new content and a separate publisher approves release. These are different responsibilities even when they use the same Knowledge app.

Verify the result

Confirm each role can perform its intended tasks and cannot perform excluded publication or editing actions. Use the same article and language when comparing users so content differences do not obscure permission differences.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If an action is missing, inspect license, feature entitlement, object and system permissions, article state, and page actions. If an article is hidden, inspect channel and category visibility before granting broad administrative access.

Limitations

Enabling Knowledge and configuring its full content model are consequential setup tasks. Access to an article in one channel or execution context does not prove it will be available to a future Agentforce data source.

Title: Draft, Publish, and Revise a Knowledge Article
Summary: Manage an article through authoring and publication while preserving the distinction between article identity and version.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Manage an article through authoring and publication while preserving the distinction between article identity and version.

Before you begin

Use an authorized Knowledge author or publisher and an existing article layout and body field. Define the intended language, internal audience, review owner, and publication checks.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Agree the support or content lifecycle with its business owner and test with synthetic customer information. Verify routing, publication, and visibility independently. A saved configuration or a success message does not prove that the intended support audience can use the result.

Steps

  1. Open Knowledge in the intended app and create a new article with the supported record type when required. Enter a descriptive title, unique URL name, language, summary, and body.
  2. Write a focused task with prerequisites, steps, verification, and limitations. Keep confidential information out of content intended for a wider audience and review formatted HTML for readability.
  3. Save the draft and review required fields, category selections, and channel visibility. Ask the designated reviewer to validate the actual procedure and target-user experience before publication.
  4. Use the supported Publish action with the intended timing and permissions. Open the resulting published version as a representative reader and confirm the correct content is visible.
  5. For a revision, use the supported action to create or edit a draft version of the existing article. Keep the logical article identity rather than creating an unrelated duplicate with a similar title.
  6. Review and publish the revision through the same process, then confirm which version readers receive. Record the content review date and retire obsolete guidance through the approved article lifecycle.

Example

A published setup procedure can remain available while an author prepares a corrected draft, depending on the chosen revision action. Check the action's publication behavior before assuming the old version stays online.

Verify the result

Confirm the draft, published status, language, URL name, and reader-visible body match the intended release. Inspect the article identity and version references when verifying a revision.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If publication is unavailable, inspect article state, required fields, entitlement, permissions, and any approval process. If readers see older content, check the published version and language before creating another article.

Limitations

Only supported draft versions can be edited directly. Creating record data does not automatically publish articles, and publication alone does not guarantee future indexing or Agentforce ingestion.

Title: Organize Knowledge with Data Categories and Visibility
Summary: Classify articles with a deliberate taxonomy and test category-based visibility separately from publication channels.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Classify articles with a deliberate taxonomy and test category-based visibility separately from publication channels.

Before you begin

Confirm Knowledge and data categories are available and obtain an approved taxonomy. Identify the intended readers and review existing category visibility before adding a new group or hierarchy.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Agree the support or content lifecycle with its business owner and test with synthetic customer information. Verify routing, publication, and visibility independently. A saved configuration or a success message does not prove that the intended support audience can use the result.

Steps

  1. In Setup, review Data Category Setup and the existing groups. Design a small hierarchy that reflects stable content concepts rather than creating a separate category for every article.
  2. Create or adjust supported category groups and categories according to the taxonomy. Activate the intended configuration and review the hierarchy before assigning content.
  3. Open a draft article and select the appropriate categories through the supported article interface. Choose the intended level and observe restrictions on selecting related ancestor and descendant categories.
  4. Configure category visibility for the relevant profiles, permission sets, or roles using the supported controls in the org. Review how those grants combine instead of assuming a category label is private by default.
  5. Review publication channels and article permissions separately. Category visibility works alongside other access conditions and is not a replacement for internal-versus-external channel decisions.
  6. Test two articles in different categories with representative authorized and unauthorized users. Document category ownership and assess future retrieval filters only after the content access model works.

Example

An internal taxonomy can separate Administration and Sales Operations guidance. If external audiences are introduced later, explicitly review channel visibility and category grants rather than assuming an internal-sounding label protects content.

Verify the result

Confirm categories are stored on the intended article version and readers see the expected articles in search and browsing. Test a category boundary with a user whose other access sources are understood.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If an article is absent, inspect publication state, language, channels, permissions, category assignment, and category visibility. If too much content is visible, trace the effective category grants rather than renaming the category.

Limitations

Taxonomy design and visibility configuration are different concerns. Future Agentforce retrieval and indexing need separate verification; categorizing and publishing an article does not configure a data library automatically.

Title: Create a Custom Report Type
Summary: Define a reusable reporting framework with the correct primary object and related-record inclusion rules.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Define a reusable reporting framework with the correct primary object and related-record inclusion rules.

Before you begin

Write the reporting question and identify the primary entity to count. Confirm object reporting support and a user with permission to manage custom report types.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Define the population and metric before changing analytics. Use known sample records to reconcile rows and totals, and test with the intended viewer. Report definitions, folder roles, and dashboard execution context are separate factors in the information a user receives.

Steps

  1. In Setup, open Report Types and select New Custom Report Type. Choose the primary object according to what one main result should represent.
  2. Enter a clear label, description, category, and development status. Keep an unfinished type In Development until the relationships and field layout have been reviewed.
  3. Add supported related objects and choose whether primary records must have a related record or may have no related record. This choice changes which records can appear in reports.
  4. Edit the report-type field layout to expose the fields report authors need. Add supported related fields through lookup relationships when appropriate and organize them into understandable sections.
  5. Create a pilot report and compare known records with and without children. Inspect whether multiple related records produce several rows for one primary record.
  6. Mark the type Deployed when validated and tell report authors what it includes. Review dependent reports before changing relationship requirements later.

Example

An Accounts with Requests type that requires a request excludes accounts with none. A type that permits accounts without requests supports a different question even when both reports show account names.

Verify the result

Test one parent with no children, one with one child, and one with several children. Confirm row counts, available fields, and inclusion behavior match the reporting question.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If records are missing, inspect relationship inclusion rules, report filters, and record access. If a field is unavailable, inspect its report-type layout, field permissions, and object support before creating a duplicate field.

Limitations

A report type defines available reporting structure rather than granting data access. Report row count can differ from the number of distinct primary records when child relationships multiply rows.

Title: Use Report Filters and Relative Date Ranges
Summary: Build a reproducible report scope and avoid misleading results caused by default ownership or date filters.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Build a reproducible report scope and avoid misleading results caused by default ownership or date filters.

Before you begin

Define the population, date field, time window, and intended viewer. Identify known records that should appear and records that must be excluded.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Define the population and metric before changing analytics. Use known sample records to reconcile rows and totals, and test with the intended viewer. Report definitions, folder roles, and dashboard execution context are separate factors in the information a user receives.

Steps

  1. Open the report in the Lightning report builder and inspect its report type. Confirm the object relationships can include the records needed for the question.
  2. Review standard scope filters such as Show Me and the selected date field. A default My Records scope or a narrow date window can exclude records before custom filters are considered.
  3. Add explicit field filters and use supported filter logic for combinations. Check blank values and the distinction between an exact value, a contains condition, and a broad text match.
  4. Choose a relative range when the report should move with time, or fixed dates when reproducing a historical selection. Check whether the range is calendar-based or fiscal-based.
  5. Run the report and compare the known included and excluded records. Inspect boundary dates and the viewing user's context where date-time values can affect interpretation.
  6. Save the report with a description of its population and time basis. Share it through the appropriate folder and test as the intended audience.

Example

A report named This Quarter Open Opportunities can still omit team records if Show Me remains My Opportunities. The title does not override the configured ownership and date filters.

Verify the result

Confirm expected records at the start and end of the range and a record outside it. Reopen the saved report and verify the persisted filters and totals match the intended definition.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If rows are missing, inspect report type, scope, date field, filter logic, object and field permissions, and sharing. If the number changes over time, check relative-date behavior before calling the report inconsistent.

Limitations

Relative dates intentionally change as time moves. A saved report is a query definition rather than a frozen historical snapshot unless its results are separately captured through an approved process.

Title: Find Records with Cross Filters
Summary: Report on primary records with or without related records without confusing the condition with a simple field filter.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Report on primary records with or without related records without confusing the condition with a simple field filter.

Before you begin

Identify a supported report type and a related-object existence question. Confirm the edition and report builder support cross filters for the intended scenario.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Define the population and metric before changing analytics. Use known sample records to reconcile rows and totals, and test with the intended viewer. Report definitions, folder roles, and dashboard execution context are separate factors in the information a user receives.

Steps

  1. Open the report in the Lightning report builder and review its primary object and existing relationships. Confirm the report can represent the required parent population.
  2. In Filters, add a Cross Filter using the available controls. Choose the primary object, related object, and WITH or WITHOUT condition according to the question.
  3. Add supported subfilters when only certain related records should count, such as open activities or requests in a particular status. Keep the existence condition separate from ordinary parent-field filters.
  4. Review all standard and custom filters together. A restrictive date or ownership scope can still exclude a parent before the cross filter produces the final result.
  5. Test known parents with no children, a matching child, and only nonmatching children. Compare the report against actual related lists or another approved record check.
  6. Save with a description of the existence rule and teach users how to interpret the output. Retest when related-status definitions change.

Example

Accounts WITHOUT open requests should include an account with only closed requests when the cross-filter subcondition defines open correctly. It is a different question from accounts with no requests of any kind.

Verify the result

Check all three known parent scenarios and verify the subfilter meaning. Confirm the report returns primary records at the intended level rather than counting unrelated child rows.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a cross filter is unavailable, inspect report-type and feature support. If results are unexpected, inspect WITH versus WITHOUT, subfilters, parent scope, and the exact child records before adding extra filter logic.

Limitations

Cross filters answer supported related-record existence questions and have limits. They do not provide an unrestricted join engine, and API-based report filtering can have different capabilities from the UI builder.

Title: Group Report Values with Bucket Fields
Summary: Create report-local categories without changing the underlying record values or schema.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Create report-local categories without changing the underlying record values or schema.

Before you begin

Choose a supported report and field whose values need reporting categories. Define a complete set of buckets and the handling of uncategorized or blank values.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Define the population and metric before changing analytics. Use known sample records to reconcile rows and totals, and test with the intended viewer. Report definitions, folder roles, and dashboard execution context are separate factors in the information a user receives.

Steps

  1. Open the report in the Lightning report builder and use the supported Add Bucket Column or field-bucketing control. Select the eligible source field.
  2. Give the bucket a descriptive label and define the category boundaries or selected values. Use nonoverlapping, business-approved ranges for numeric data.
  3. Review the treatment of blanks and values outside named buckets. Make the remaining category explicit so the report does not hide an unclassified population.
  4. Add the bucket to the report as a column or grouping where supported. Compare the displayed classifications with the original field on a small known set of records.
  5. Test boundary values, a blank, and an unexpected category. For numeric ranges, calculate which bucket each boundary should enter before relying on the displayed totals.
  6. Save with a description of the categorization rule. Review whether several reports need a shared classification; repeated independent buckets may indicate a separate schema requirement.

Example

A report can group estimated request amounts into Small, Medium, and Large without writing those labels back to the request. Another report can use different buckets unless the team deliberately standardizes them.

Verify the result

Confirm every known sample appears in the correct bucket and the total row population remains understood. Compare grouped totals with the same report before bucketing.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If an expected value is uncategorized, inspect the bucket membership or range boundaries. If the feature is unavailable, inspect field and report support rather than changing the underlying data type just for one chart.

Limitations

Bucket fields are report definitions rather than stored record fields. They do not validate data entry, update business records, or automatically provide a reusable classification to integrations.

Title: Summarize and Visualize Report Data
Summary: Use groupings, summaries, and a chart to answer a defined question without double-counting records.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Use groupings, summaries, and a chart to answer a defined question without double-counting records.

Before you begin

Define the metric, grouping, and time window. Determine whether the result should count report rows, distinct primary records, or a sum of a numeric field.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Define the population and metric before changing analytics. Use known sample records to reconcile rows and totals, and test with the intended viewer. Report definitions, folder roles, and dashboard execution context are separate factors in the information a user receives.

Steps

  1. Open the report in the Lightning report builder and confirm its filters and report type. Inspect a few detail rows before introducing summaries.
  2. Add a row grouping for the primary comparison and a column grouping where a matrix-style analysis is useful and supported. Keep groupings aligned with the reporting question.
  3. Add the appropriate summary to an eligible numeric field, such as Sum or Average. Use record counts carefully when the report type can create multiple rows per primary record.
  4. Add a supported chart and choose a visualization that matches the metric. A bar chart suits comparing categories; a trend needs a meaningful time grouping and consistent periods.
  5. Review chart labels, axis units, currency, and blank categories. Confirm that a visible total is not distorted by child-row duplication or a summary of an already repeated parent value.
  6. Save and compare the chart with manually checked groups. Ask a representative reader to explain what one bar or point means before using it in an operational dashboard.

Example

A requests-by-status chart can count requests, while a report joining each request to several child lines may count rows instead. The same title does not make those two counts equivalent.

Verify the result

Calculate one group by hand and reconcile overall totals with a known population. Confirm the chart uses the intended summary and that grouping changes do not silently change the metric definition.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a chart is unavailable, inspect report format, grouping, and supported data. If totals are inflated, inspect report-type relationships and repeated values rather than changing the chart scale.

Limitations

Charts summarize the report's actual rows and visibility. They do not correct unsuitable joins, misleading filters, or a metric whose business definition has not been agreed.

Title: Add a Row-Level or Summary Formula to a Report
Summary: Choose a report formula that calculates at the appropriate level and test its meaning.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Choose a report formula that calculates at the appropriate level and test its meaning.

Before you begin

Write the expected calculation and identify whether it applies to each detail row or an aggregated group. Confirm the report and field types support the intended formula.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Define the population and metric before changing analytics. Use known sample records to reconcile rows and totals, and test with the intended viewer. Report definitions, folder roles, and dashboard execution context are separate factors in the information a user receives.

Steps

  1. Open the report in the Lightning report builder and inspect available formula options. Choose a row-level formula for a per-row result or a summary formula for a grouped calculation.
  2. Select the return type and build the expression with the editor's supported field and function selectors. Use the report formula syntax rather than assuming every object-formula expression works unchanged.
  3. Define blank, zero, and denominator handling. For percentages, decide whether the requirement is an average of row percentages or a ratio of totals; these can produce different answers.
  4. For a summary formula, select the grouping levels at which the result should display. Review grand-total behavior separately from individual groups.
  5. Validate and run the report with a small known dataset. Check individual values, group values, and the grand total against hand calculations.
  6. Save the report and document the formula's business meaning and limitations. Recheck the expression when report type, groupings, or included fields change.

Example

A ratio of total won amount to total amount is not generally the same as averaging a percentage calculated on every row. The metric owner must choose the intended calculation before selecting the formula level.

Verify the result

Test normal inputs, zero or missing inputs, multiple groups, and the overall total. Confirm formatting and decimal precision make the result understandable without obscuring a calculation error.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If syntax fails, inspect supported fields, functions, grouping references, and return types. If the total seems wrong, inspect formula level and row duplication before adjusting the expression to match an expected-looking number.

Limitations

Report formulas are report-local calculations and have type-specific limits. They do not store a new business value on the original record or enforce data-entry rules.

Title: Share Report and Dashboard Folders
Summary: Give the intended audience access to saved analytics with an appropriate folder role.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Give the intended audience access to saved analytics with an appropriate folder role.

Before you begin

Identify whether users should view, edit, or manage the folder. Review existing folder content and audience because sharing a folder can expose more than one report or dashboard definition.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Define the population and metric before changing analytics. Use known sample records to reconcile rows and totals, and test with the intended viewer. Report definitions, folder roles, and dashboard execution context are separate factors in the information a user receives.

Steps

  1. Open Reports or Dashboards and find the relevant folder. Use its Share control with a user authorized to manage the folder.
  2. Choose the supported users, groups, or roles and select the least folder access level that fits the requirement. Distinguish Viewer, Editor, and Manager responsibilities.
  3. Review all reports or dashboards in the folder before broadening its audience. Move unrelated or sensitive definitions into an appropriate separately managed location when necessary.
  4. Share source-report folders where dashboard use or maintenance requires access. Check dashboard viewing and running-user behavior separately rather than assuming folder roles describe all data exposure.
  5. Test with a representative viewer and editor. Confirm viewers can run intended analytics and editors can modify only what their role and other permissions allow.
  6. Record a folder owner and review date. Remove obsolete grants and recheck access when team membership or public-group nesting changes.

Example

A Sales Operations group can receive Editor access to a reporting folder while managers receive Viewer access. Giving every consumer Manager rights would also let them alter the folder's sharing configuration.

Verify the result

Confirm each test user can find and open the saved content and the permitted editing behavior matches the assigned role. Verify the underlying data and dashboard context separately.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If a report is missing, inspect its actual saved folder and sharing grants. If it opens with no rows, inspect filters, object permissions, field permissions, and record access rather than increasing the folder role.

Limitations

Folder access controls saved analytics content. It does not automatically grant access to all underlying records, and a fixed-running-user dashboard can disclose data under a different visibility context.

Title: Choose a Dashboard Running User Safely
Summary: Decide whose data visibility a dashboard uses and verify the result with its intended audience.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Decide whose data visibility a dashboard uses and verify the result with its intended audience.

Before you begin

Define whether viewers should see a shared business view or only their own permitted data. Confirm dynamic-dashboard availability and limits, and inventory the source reports and folder audience.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Define the population and metric before changing analytics. Use known sample records to reconcile rows and totals, and test with the intended viewer. Report definitions, folder roles, and dashboard execution context are separate factors in the information a user receives.

Steps

  1. Open the dashboard in edit mode and inspect its viewing or running-user properties. Identify whether it currently uses a named user or the dashboard viewer.
  2. For a fixed running user, choose a suitable active user whose visibility matches the approved dashboard audience. Avoid selecting a highly privileged administrator merely to make every component show data.
  3. For a dynamic dashboard where supported, choose the viewer-based option. Review any permissions that let viewers change the perspective and confirm the intended restrictions.
  4. Review every component and source report for sensitive totals and filters. Folder access and source-report access should be considered alongside the chosen execution context.
  5. Save and test with two users who have different record visibility. Compare their displayed metrics with known data and confirm whether differences or identical totals are expected by design.
  6. Document the running-user owner and reassess dashboards when that user changes roles or leaves. Include subscriptions, refresh behavior, and supported dynamic-dashboard constraints in the operating process.

Example

A fixed-user dashboard shared broadly can show aggregate data that viewers could not retrieve in their own reports. That may be appropriate for an approved summary, but it must be an explicit sharing decision.

Verify the result

Check the configured perspective and compare metrics for users with different access. Verify a known sensitive record contributes only when the approved dashboard design permits its information to appear.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If totals differ from a viewer's report, inspect running user, filters, refresh time, and source report definitions. If a dashboard fails after staffing changes, inspect the active status and permissions of its named running user.

Limitations

Dashboard execution context can disclose broader aggregates than the viewer's own records. Dynamic-dashboard availability, refresh, scheduling, and subscription capabilities vary, so verify the target org's supported options.

Title: Subscribe to Reports and Dashboards
Summary: Schedule supported analytics notifications and verify recipients, data context, and delivery.
Article_Body__c:
Purpose

Schedule supported analytics notifications and verify recipients, data context, and delivery.

Before you begin

Confirm subscription features are available for the user and analytics type. Identify the audience, approved schedule, data sensitivity, and whether recipients are allowed to receive the information by email.

Use Lightning Experience and an account authorized for this task. Try configuration changes in a development or test org before production. Available options depend on edition, licenses, enabled features, and release. Record the current configuration so the change can be reviewed.

Define the population and metric before changing analytics. Use known sample records to reconcile rows and totals, and test with the intended viewer. Report definitions, folder roles, and dashboard execution context are separate factors in the information a user receives.

Steps

  1. Open the saved report or dashboard and inspect Subscribe or the equivalent supported notification control. Verify the content is saved in an accessible folder and runs correctly first.
  2. Configure the supported schedule, frequency, and conditions. Review the time-zone interpretation shown by the interface so users know when to expect the notification.
  3. Choose recipients only where the feature and permissions permit it. Confirm their access and the execution context used to produce the notification rather than assuming every recipient sees their own personalized result.
  4. Review email or attachment options and the sensitivity of included data. A delivered message can be forwarded or retained outside Salesforce, so use the organization's approved distribution policy.
  5. Save and test a controlled notification where supported, or monitor the next scheduled delivery. Compare received content with the intended report filters, dashboard perspective, and refresh state.
  6. Document the subscription owner and review it when people leave or the report changes. Remove obsolete recipients and investigate failures before creating duplicate subscriptions.

Example

A weekly pipeline email should use the intended date range and permitted audience. A dashboard notification based on a shared running-user perspective should not be described as each recipient's personal pipeline without testing that assumption.

Verify the result

Confirm the saved schedule, recipients, execution context, and received content. Check condition-based notifications both when the condition matches and when no notification should be produced.

Keep the sample record identifiers where applicable, expected result, observed result, and test user with the review notes. Repeat the key scenario in the destination environment because permissions, assignments, and enabled features can differ.

Troubleshooting

If no message arrives, inspect feature permissions, subscription limits, conditions, scheduling, recipient eligibility, and email delivery. If results appear stale, inspect report filters and dashboard refresh behavior before duplicating the schedule.

Limitations

Report and dashboard subscriptions have different capabilities and limits, and some dynamic-dashboard scenarios restrict scheduling. A subscription does not grant folder or record access or guarantee delivery to an external mail system.
